Chapter 119: Natural Care in the Third Stage After Birth

My dear,

Natural or physiological management of the third stage of labor means waiting for the placenta to separate and deliver spontaneously without the use of uterotonic medicines and without cord traction. This approach relies on the mother's own oxytocin, released naturally through skin-to-skin contact and early breastfeeding, to stimulate effective uterine contractions.

In the natural approach, the cord is not clamped until it has stopped pulsating, which typically takes three to five minutes. The baby remains skin-to-skin on the mother throughout, which optimizes the natural oxytocin release. Gravity assists when the mother is in an upright position. The mother pushes the placenta out with her own effort when the bearing-down urge returns.

Natural management of the third stage has several theoretical advantages. It avoids the pharmacological side effects of oxytocin medicines, which can include nausea, headache, and in high doses cardiovascular effects. It allows maximum cord blood transfusion to the baby. It respects the physiological process of birth when that process is working normally.

However, natural management is associated with a higher rate of postpartum hemorrhage compared to active management. In settings where blood transfusion and emergency obstetric care are immediately accessible and the woman is at low risk, natural management is a reasonable option for women who choose it after informed discussion.

In most clinical settings, particularly in lower-resource environments or where the ability to respond rapidly to hemorrhage is limited, active management is recommended as the safer standard. The choice between natural and active management should be made in discussion with the woman, with clear information about the evidence for each approach, and with safety as the primary guide.

Chapter 120: Active Care in the Third Stage to Reduce Bleeding

My dear,

Active management of the third stage is a set of evidence-based interventions that significantly reduces the risk of postpartum hemorrhage compared to expectant management. It is recommended by the World Health Organization for all deliveries as the standard of care.

Active management consists of three components. The first and most important is the administration of a uterotonic medicine within one minute of the baby's birth. Oxytocin ten international units given by intramuscular injection into the thigh is the preferred uterotonic. It causes the uterus to contract strongly, which compresses the blood vessels where the placenta was attached and dramatically reduces bleeding. Where oxytocin is unavailable or requires refrigeration that cannot be guaranteed, other uterotonics including misoprostol may be used.

The second component is controlled cord traction. After the uterus has contracted well following the uterotonic injection, and signs of placental separation are present, the care provider places one hand above the pubic bone to support the uterus and exerts controlled traction on the cord with the other hand to deliver the placenta. This technique, called Brandt-Andrews maneuver, reduces the time to placental delivery and reduces blood loss. Cord traction should never be applied without a well-contracted uterus and clear signs of separation, as doing so risks inverting the uterus, a rare but life-threatening complication.

The third component is uterine massage after delivery of the placenta, palpating and massaging the fundus of the uterus to maintain and stimulate its contraction.

Active management reduces severe postpartum hemorrhage by approximately sixty percent compared to expectant management. In a context where postpartum hemorrhage remains a leading cause of maternal death, this reduction represents an enormous benefit. Every delivery should include the offer and provision of active third stage management.

Chapter 121: Checking the Baby's Feeding Organ and Coverings

My dear,

Immediately after the placenta is delivered, the placenta and membranes are carefully examined to ensure they are complete. This examination is a routine but important step in third stage management.

The placenta is a round or oval disc typically weighing approximately five hundred to six hundred grams at term. Its maternal surface, the side that was attached to the uterine wall, has a rough, lobulated appearance divided into segments called cotyledons. Its fetal surface, the side facing the baby, is smooth and covered by the amnion, the inner membrane. The umbilical cord inserts into the fetal surface.

Each cotyledon on the maternal surface is counted or assessed to confirm the placenta is complete. Missing cotyledons suggest a fragment has been retained in the uterus, which is a cause of ongoing or delayed postpartum hemorrhage and infection requiring further management.

The membranes, the amniotic sac, are examined to confirm that both layers, the amnion and chorion, appear complete. Ragged or incomplete membranes suggest retained membrane tissue.

The umbilical cord is examined. It normally contains three vessels: two arteries and one vein. A two-vessel cord, containing only one artery and one vein, is associated with a higher rate of fetal structural abnormalities and should be noted in the birth records. It does not in itself require emergency action but is relevant information for the newborn assessment.

When any doubt exists about placental or membrane completeness, the woman requires careful monitoring for bleeding and possible assessment including ultrasound. Manual removal of retained placenta under appropriate anaesthesia may be required if the placenta has not delivered completely and bleeding is occurring.

Documentation of placental examination is mandatory in the birth records.

Chapter 122: Checking and Repairing Cuts After Birth

My dear,

After the delivery of the placenta and completion of the third stage, the perineum, vaginal walls, and cervix are carefully examined for tears or lacerations. Repairing these injuries promptly and correctly is important for the mother's recovery, comfort, and long-term pelvic health.

Perineal tears are classified by degree. A first-degree tear involves only the skin and superficial tissues and may not require suturing. A second-degree tear involves the skin and the perineal muscles and requires repair with absorbable sutures. A third-degree tear extends into the anal sphincter, the muscle that controls bowel movements, and requires specialist repair by a trained surgeon. A fourth-degree tear extends completely through the anal sphincter and into the rectal mucosa and requires careful surgical repair in theatre.

Third and fourth-degree tears, called obstetric anal sphincter injuries, are associated with long-term problems including anal incontinence if not recognized and repaired correctly. Identifying them requires thorough examination of the extent of the tear, which must include a rectal examination to assess the sphincter complex. These injuries are more common when the baby is large, when forceps or vacuum delivery is used, when the delivery is precipitate, and in women having their first baby.

Repair is performed under local anaesthesia in first and second-degree tears. Third and fourth-degree tears are repaired in theatre under regional or general anaesthesia. The quality of the repair matters enormously for long-term outcomes.

Episiotomy, a deliberate surgical cut of the perineum made when necessary to facilitate delivery or prevent an uncontrolled tear in a specific direction, is also repaired in layers with absorbable suture after birth.

All women should be told what was found and what was repaired, and given clear guidance about perineal care and symptoms to watch for in the recovery period.

Chapter 123: Family Planning Device Placed Soon After Birth

My dear,

The immediate postpartum period, the hours and days following birth, is an important window for family planning counseling and in some cases for initiating a contraceptive method. Women are highly motivated to consider family planning immediately after birth, and a conversation in this period can provide protection during a time when unplanned pregnancy can have significant health consequences.

An intrauterine contraceptive device can be inserted within ten minutes of delivery of the placenta, before the uterus has fully involuted. This timing, called postplacental insertion, is simple for an experienced provider because the uterus is open and the cervix is dilated. Postplacental insertion is associated with good continuation rates and avoids the risk of the woman returning home without contraception and then not coming back for a device.

An intrauterine device inserted immediately after birth does have a slightly higher rate of expulsion compared to interval insertion, meaning more devices pass out of the uterus in the following weeks. The woman must be counseled to check the device strings after her first postpartum period and to return if she cannot feel them.

Implants can also be inserted immediately postpartum. An implant placed in the upper arm in the delivery room or postnatal ward provides three years of highly effective contraception and can be done before the woman leaves the facility.

Breastfeeding itself provides a natural family planning effect called the Lactation Amenorrhea Method when the baby is exclusively breastfed, periods have not returned, and the baby is less than six months old. When all three conditions are met, the pregnancy rate is low but not zero, and it is not recommended as the sole method.

All postnatal contraceptive decisions should be made freely, with full information about options, their effectiveness, and how to access them, without pressure or coercion.

Chapter 124: Immediate Care of the Tender Area Below

My dear,

The perineum, the area between the vaginal opening and the anus, undergoes significant stress during birth. Whether or not there was a tear or episiotomy, the perineum is typically tender, swollen, and bruised immediately after birth. Caring for this area properly in the first hours and days supports comfortable recovery.

In the first hours after birth, applying ice wrapped in a clean cloth to the perineum for fifteen to twenty minutes at a time reduces swelling and provides significant pain relief. Direct application of ice without wrapping causes ice burns on the tender skin. The cold compress should be available to every woman who has given birth vaginally, regardless of whether a repair was performed.

Keeping the perineal area clean is important to prevent infection of any tear or repair. Gentle washing with clean warm water after every toilet visit, patting dry rather than rubbing, and changing sanitary pads frequently keeps the area clean and reduces infection risk.

Positioning matters for comfort. Sitting on a soft cushion, donut-shaped cushion, or a folded soft towel reduces direct pressure on the perineum during sitting. Some women find sitting on the side, taking weight on the buttocks unevenly, more comfortable in the first days.

Constipation after birth causes significant perineal discomfort and can put strain on a repair. Ensuring adequate fluid intake, eating high-fiber food, using a stool softener if prescribed, and not delaying going to the toilet when the urge is felt all prevent constipation and the associated straining.

A warm sitz bath, where the woman sits in a few inches of warm water, provides excellent pain relief and promotes healing for the perineal area. It can be done in a bath or in a shallow basin.

Pain that is worsening rather than improving, significant swelling, a feeling of pressure or fullness in the perineum, or any discharge with an unusual smell from the repair area should be reported to the care team.

Chapter 125: Starting Breastfeeding Early After Birth

My dear,

Initiating breastfeeding in the first hour after birth is one of the most powerful steps toward successful, sustained breastfeeding. This window is called the golden hour, and its importance rests on both the physiology of milk supply establishment and the remarkable behavioural state of the newborn in the first hour.

A healthy newborn in the first hour after birth is typically alert, wide-eyed, and actively searching for the breast. This is the baby's first and most sustained wakeful period in the first days. In this alert state, the baby has strong, coordinated sucking reflexes, and skin-to-skin contact with the mother on her bare chest in this period stimulates the baby's instinctive breast-seeking behavior.

The first feed in the hours after birth is of colostrum, the early form of breast milk. Colostrum is yellow to orange in color, thick, and produced only in small quantities. This small quantity is intentional and perfectly matched to the tiny stomach capacity of the newborn. Colostrum is extraordinarily rich in antibodies, white blood cells, growth factors, and concentrated nutrients. It provides essential immune protection in the baby's first days and primes the gut for mature milk production.

The sucking of the baby at the breast in the first hours after birth stimulates the release of prolactin, which signals the breasts to make milk, and oxytocin, which helps the uterus contract and reduce postpartum bleeding. The earlier and more frequently the baby suckles, the more effectively and abundantly the milk supply establishes.

Giving the baby formula, sugar water, or any other supplement in the first hours and days undermines this process by reducing the baby's hunger and frequency of feeding at the breast. Unless there is a genuine clinical indication for supplementation, exclusive breastfeeding from the first feed is the gold standard recommendation for every healthy mother-baby pair.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 126: Skin-to-Skin Touch After Birth

My dear,

Skin-to-skin contact between mother and newborn, placing the naked baby directly on the mother's bare chest immediately after birth, is one of the most evidence-supported practices in all of newborn care. Its benefits for both the baby and the mother begin within minutes of birth and continue for days and weeks afterward.

For the baby, skin-to-skin contact maintains body temperature more effectively than any warmer or incubator when the baby is healthy. The mother's skin temperature adjusts dynamically in response to the baby's needs. The baby in skin-to-skin contact has more stable blood sugar, more regular breathing and heart rate, lower cortisol levels indicating less stress, and is more likely to initiate breastfeeding spontaneously.

Skin-to-skin contact with the mother exposes the baby to the mother's own skin bacteria, which colonize the baby's gut and immune system. These bacteria are associated with lower rates of infection and allergy in infancy compared to the bacteria a baby encounters when separated into a crib or warmer.

For the mother, skin-to-skin contact stimulates oxytocin release, which reduces postpartum bleeding, supports uterine involution, and promotes the emotional bonding experience of early motherhood. The skin contact also initiates the release of prolactin for milk production.

Skin-to-skin contact should begin immediately after birth, before the cord is cut in healthy births, and should continue uninterrupted for at least the first hour or until after the first successful breastfeed, whichever is longer. Routine newborn procedures including weighing, measuring, and administering vitamin K should be deferred until after this initial uninterrupted skin-to-skin period in healthy newborns.

When the mother is unable to have skin-to-skin contact due to illness or surgical recovery, the father or another family member can provide skin-to-skin care, which carries similar benefits for the baby's stability and warmth.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 127: Helping a Baby Start Breathing

My dear,

The vast majority of healthy newborns, approximately ninety percent, begin breathing spontaneously and effectively within the first minute of birth. They require only drying, warmth, and skin-to-skin contact to establish independent breathing. However, approximately ten percent require some assistance to breathe effectively, and about one to two percent require more active resuscitation. Every birth team must be prepared to provide this assistance.

The first response to a baby who is not breathing spontaneously after birth is warmth, drying, and stimulation. Thorough drying with a dry warm towel provides the stimulation that often triggers the first breath in a baby who has not breathed spontaneously. Positioning the baby on a flat, warm surface with the head in a slightly neutral position to open the airway and clearing visible secretions from the mouth and nose are the next steps.

If the baby remains apneic, limp, or has a heart rate below one hundred beats per minute after this initial stimulation, positive pressure ventilation is initiated. A tight-fitting mask connected to a bag is placed over the baby's mouth and nose and gentle, controlled breaths are delivered at a rate of approximately forty per minute. The effectiveness of ventilation is assessed by watching the chest rise with each breath and by reassessing the heart rate every thirty seconds.

For most babies requiring resuscitation, effective positive pressure ventilation alone is sufficient. The heart rate rises, color improves, and spontaneous breathing begins.

A small number of babies require more extensive resuscitation including chest compressions and medicines if the heart rate remains very low despite effective ventilation. This requires a team with resuscitation training and appropriate equipment.

The vast majority of births can be made safe through preparedness, early action on warning signs during pregnancy, and the presence of at least one skilled person at every birth capable of providing initial newborn resuscitation.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 128: The Fourth Stage: Watching Mother and Baby Closely

My dear,

The first one to two hours after delivery of the placenta is sometimes called the fourth stage of labor. This period carries a disproportionately high risk of postpartum hemorrhage, the most common serious complication of childbirth. Almost half of all maternal deaths from hemorrhage occur in the first hour after birth, which is why close monitoring during this period is not optional.

For the mother, monitoring in the fourth stage includes blood pressure and pulse every fifteen minutes for the first hour and every thirty minutes for the second hour. Vital signs that are changing, particularly a rising pulse and falling blood pressure, are early warning signs of hemorrhage. The fundus of the uterus is palpated regularly to confirm it is firm and contracting. A soft, poorly contracted uterus in the first hours after birth is the primary cause of postpartum hemorrhage and requires immediate massage and repeat uterotonic medicine.

Blood loss is observed and estimated. Pads are checked regularly. A woman who is soaking more than one pad per hour in the first hours after birth is losing significant blood volume and needs urgent assessment.

The woman's level of consciousness, ability to communicate, and comfort are assessed continuously. She should be with someone at all times during the fourth stage.

For the baby, the heart rate, respiratory rate, skin color, temperature, and feeding behavior are monitored. The blood sugar of babies at risk of hypoglycemia, including those of diabetic mothers, premature babies, and those who are small for gestational age, is measured in the first hours.

This critical period requires full attention from the care team. It is not the time for documentation at a desk, breaks, or reduced vigilance. The lives of both mother and baby depend on what is noticed and acted upon in these first hours.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 129: Checking the Mother Carefully After Birth

My dear,

After the immediate fourth stage monitoring period, a systematic postnatal examination confirms that the mother is recovering normally and identifies any concerns requiring further attention before she is transferred to a postnatal ward or discharged home.

Vital signs are measured and compared to pre-delivery values. Blood pressure should be returning toward normal if it was elevated during labor. Persistent high blood pressure in the postpartum period continues to carry risk and requires continued monitoring and treatment. Pulse should be settling toward the normal range. Temperature is measured to screen for early signs of infection.

The uterus is palpated. It should feel firm, round, and located roughly at the level of the umbilicus immediately after birth, progressively decreasing in size over the following days. A soft, tender, or significantly enlarged uterus suggests poor involution and the possibility of retained tissue or infection.

The amount and character of vaginal discharge, called lochia, is assessed. Normal lochia is red and bloodstained in the first three days, transitioning to pink or brown in the following week, and then to yellow-white. Heavy, foul-smelling, or unusually persisting red lochia is not normal and warrants assessment.

The perineum is inspected. Any repair should be intact, with wound edges coming together. Signs of infection, significant swelling, or a hematoma forming under the repair tissue should be documented and managed.

The legs are examined for swelling, redness, or warmth that might suggest a venous clot. Women who had prolonged labor, surgical delivery, or significant immobility are at higher risk.

The woman's pain is assessed and managed. Adequate pain relief in the postnatal period is a clinical priority that supports early mobility, breastfeeding, and emotional recovery. Undertreated pain is not an acceptable aspect of postpartum care.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 130: Writing Down the Birth Details Properly

My dear,

Complete, accurate documentation of the birth and immediate postpartum period is both a legal requirement and a clinical safety tool. A birth record that is clear, accurate, and complete serves every person who will subsequently care for the mother or baby, and provides an irreplaceable account of what happened in the event of complications or questions.

The birth record must document the date and time of birth, the mode of delivery, who conducted the delivery, the baby's condition at birth including Apgar scores at one and five minutes, the weight and sex, any procedures performed including episiotomy or instrumental delivery, the management of the third stage, the time of placental delivery and whether it was complete, the estimated blood loss, any medicines given and their doses and times, the condition of the perineum and any repair performed, and the condition of the mother immediately after birth.

For the newborn, documentation includes the birth weight, length and head circumference, Apgar scores, immediate resuscitation if required, skin-to-skin contact, the first breastfeed, and any medicines given including vitamin K.

All examination findings in the fourth stage, including vital signs at their designated intervals, uterine palpation results, and lochia assessment, are recorded with the time of each observation.

When complications occurred during labor or delivery, detailed documentation is even more critical. The sequence of events, the clinical findings at each assessment, the decisions made and why, and the immediate outcomes must all be recorded clearly and honestly. This documentation protects the mother when she needs care at a different facility, protects the clinical team in the event of legal or audit questions, and provides the data needed for quality improvement of maternity services.

Documentation is not a burden. It is a responsibility that directly serves the people being cared for.
With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 131: Breastfeeding and Correct Baby Attachment

My dear,

The difference between breastfeeding that is comfortable, effective, and successful, and breastfeeding that is painful, frustrating, and eventually abandoned, often comes down to one factor: whether the baby is correctly attached to the breast.

Correct attachment means the baby takes a large mouthful of breast tissue, not just the nipple. The baby's mouth should be wide open, with lips flanged outward like a fish's mouth rather than pursed inward. The baby's chin should be touching the breast. More areola should be visible above the baby's upper lip than below the lower lip.

When the baby is well attached, the mother should feel a strong tugging sensation during sucking but no pain. Breastfeeding should never be consistently painful. Pain indicates incorrect attachment. The most common mistake is allowing the baby to suck only on the nipple, which causes nipple soreness, cracking, and bleeding within days, and does not allow the baby to extract milk effectively.

Correct positioning of the mother and baby supports correct attachment. The baby's entire body should face the mother, tummy to tummy. The head, shoulders, and hips should be aligned, not twisted. The baby should come to the breast nose to nipple, tilting the head back slightly to achieve a wide gape, rather than being pushed face-first onto the breast.

The first sign that a baby is getting milk is audible swallowing. Slow, rhythmic, deep sucks with visible movement of the jaw and regular swallowing confirm effective milk transfer. A baby who is attached well, feeding actively, and swallowing regularly will produce several wet nappies per day and gain weight as expected.

Every mother deserves hands-on breastfeeding support from a skilled healthcare worker in the first hours and days after birth. Correct attachment, taught once in the first feed and reinforced at subsequent feeds, prevents the majority of early breastfeeding problems.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 132: Understanding Womb Cramps After Birth

My dear,

After birth, the uterus does not simply relax and remain at its delivery size. It must contract repeatedly and progressively over the days and weeks following birth to return to its pre-pregnancy size and to stop the bleeding from the site where the placenta was attached. This process, called uterine involution, involves significant rhythmic contractions that many women experience as cramps.

These postpartum cramps, sometimes called afterpains, are felt as period-like cramps in the lower abdomen. They are typically most intense in the first two to three days after birth and gradually ease over the following week. In women who have given birth before, the cramps tend to be more noticeable because the uterus has less natural tone and must work harder to maintain contraction.

The cramps are often most prominent during breastfeeding. This is because breastfeeding stimulates the release of oxytocin, which is the hormone that drives uterine contractions. This connection between breastfeeding and afterpains is beneficial for the mother because the strong uterine contractions it causes reduce postpartum bleeding and speed up the return of the uterus to its normal size. Telling mothers about this connection helps them understand why cramps during feeding are normal and expected rather than a sign that something is wrong.

For most women, afterpains are managed with the same mild pain relievers used for period cramps, specifically paracetamol or ibuprofen. These medicines are safe during breastfeeding when used at standard doses. Applying warmth to the lower abdomen provides additional comfort.

Severe, worsening, or persistently one-sided pain after birth, particularly if accompanied by fever, is not normal afterpain and needs medical review to exclude infection or other complications.
With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 133: Safe Supportive Therapies After Birth

My dear,

The postpartum period is a time when many women and families seek additional supportive care alongside clinical care. Understanding which supportive therapies are safe, beneficial, and evidence-based, and which carry risks, helps families make informed choices.

Warmth is one of the oldest and most universally applied postnatal practices. Traditional postpartum practices across South Asia, East Asia, and many African cultures involve keeping the mother warm, sometimes to a significant degree. The principle of avoiding cold drafts and keeping the body warm after birth has a physiological basis: the body is recovering from significant fluid loss, hormonal shifts, and physical exertion, and warmth supports recovery. However, excessive heat particularly to the perineum, including practices such as sitting over hot steam, carries the risk of burns and infection. Gentle warmth without direct heat application to the perineal area is safe.

Massage is widely used in postpartum recovery in India, often including abdominal massage to help the uterus contract. Gentle abdominal massage has a physiological basis in supporting involution. Massage should be gentle, performed with clean hands, and should avoid direct pressure on any incision sites including cesarean wounds. Professional trained postpartum massage is beneficial for muscle recovery and emotional wellbeing.

Rest is the most important and most frequently denied postnatal supportive therapy. The mother who is expected to be actively caring for the household and visitors while recovering from birth is not receiving adequate postnatal support. A minimum of six weeks of significantly reduced physical work, with family support for cooking, cleaning, and childcare of older children, is not cultural indulgence. It is genuine recovery care that protects long-term maternal health.

Traditional dietary practices after birth vary enormously between cultures. Those that emphasize nutritious, warm, easily digested food support recovery. Those that excessively restrict dietary variety may contribute to nutritional deficiencies during a period of high need.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 134: How Doula and ASHA Help Around Birth

My dear,

The doula and the ASHA worker contribute differently to the birth period, and both provide forms of support that the clinical team alone cannot replicate.

In the labor room, the doula's continuous presence provides the evidence-based benefits of labor companionship described in previous chapters: shorter labors, fewer interventions, better pain management, and higher maternal satisfaction. After birth, the doula supports the mother through the first breastfeed, helps with skin-to-skin positioning, explains what the clinical team is doing during the immediate newborn assessment, and provides emotional support during the vulnerable first hours. A doula present through labor and the immediate postpartum period helps the mother feel witnessed, supported, and remembered as a person rather than a patient.

The ASHA's contribution is strongest in the period before and after birth rather than during labor itself. Before birth, ASHA workers identify women who have not yet entered antenatal care and support their enrollment. They arrange transport to the facility when labor begins, which is critically important in rural and poorly connected communities where delays in reaching care are a leading cause of preventable maternal death. After birth, ASHA workers visit the home in the days following discharge to check on the mother and baby, support breastfeeding continuation, refer any warning signs to the nearest health facility, and ensure that the newborn vaccination schedule begins on time.

Both roles are most effective when they work in genuine partnership with the clinical team rather than in parallel or in conflict. A facility that welcomes ASHA workers and doulas, shares information with them, and recognizes their contribution, builds a care system that surrounds the mother from community to clinic and back again.

Chapter 135: Childbirth Practices: What Helps and What Harms

My dear,

Childbirth is surrounded by practices that have been passed from generation to generation, some of which actively support safe birth and some of which carry genuine risk. A thoughtful review of common practices in the Indian context helps families make safer choices.

Practices that help: Institutional delivery attended by skilled healthcare workers, which reduces maternal and newborn mortality dramatically. Immediate skin-to-skin contact after birth, which supports temperature, breathing, blood sugar, and breastfeeding. Delayed cord clamping, which improves iron stores in the baby. Active management of the third stage, which prevents hemorrhage. Early exclusive breastfeeding, which protects against infection. Vitamin K for the newborn, which prevents a rare but serious bleeding condition. Adequate maternal rest in the postpartum period. Warm, clean environment for both mother and baby.

Practices that harm: Applying pressure to the fundus during second stage labor, called fundal pressure, which carries risk of uterine rupture and is not recommended. Application of harmful substances to the umbilical cord stump including ash, cow dung, or herbal preparations, which causes serious infection. Withholding colostrum and giving the baby sugar water, honey, or formula before breastfeeding is established, which increases infection risk and undermines milk supply. Restriction of fluids or food from the laboring woman without medical indication, which increases fatigue and dehydration. Separation of the healthy newborn from the mother without clinical reason. Premature bathing of the newborn, which removes the protective vernix and causes heat loss.

Neutral practices that are culturally important but do not harm: Religious or spiritual rituals performed after birth that do not involve applying substances to the baby, that maintain hygiene, and that support the mother's emotional wellbeing are culturally valuable and need not be discouraged.

Chapter 136: A Safe Place for Mother and Baby to Bond

My dear,

Bonding between mother and newborn is not a single event that either happens or does not happen at birth. It is a process that develops through repeated interactions of touch, feeding, eye contact, response to the baby's signals, and the mother's growing knowledge of her specific baby. Understanding this removes the excessive anxiety many mothers feel when bonding does not feel instantaneous.

The conditions that support bonding are simple and should be actively created. Privacy between the mother and baby, uninterrupted time together in the first hours after birth, skin-to-skin contact, breastfeeding, and low disturbance from well-meaning visitors and clinical procedures all allow the bonding process to begin without interference.

Separation of mother and baby without clinical reason directly undermines bonding. When a healthy newborn is placed in a separate nursery rather than staying in the mother's room, the frequency of their interactions decreases, the mother loses confidence in understanding her baby's signals, and breastfeeding is harder to establish. Rooming-in, where the healthy newborn stays in the same room as the mother throughout the hospital stay, supports bonding, facilitates on-demand breastfeeding, and reduces infection risk compared to nursery care.

For mothers who experienced a difficult birth, who had significant blood loss, who underwent cesarean section, or who are unwell themselves, bonding may be slower to develop. These mothers need compassionate reassurance that the bond will grow and patience from the care team and family. The baby's safety may mean brief separation while the mother recovers, but skin-to-skin contact should begin as soon as it is safely possible.

For mothers experiencing postnatal mental health difficulties including postpartum depression, professional support alongside compassionate practical help from the family creates the conditions needed for bonding to develop at its own pace.

Chapter 137: Keeping Records and Reports After Delivery

My dear,

The documentation generated at delivery is not only for the clinical team's benefit. It serves the mother, the newborn, the wider health system, and any future caregivers. Maintaining complete, accurate, and accessible records after delivery is a professional and ethical obligation.

The case notes from the labor and delivery are the primary clinical record. They include the labor timeline, progress assessments, interventions performed, medicines given, the birth details, the immediate newborn assessment, and the third stage management. These notes must be legible, dated, timed, and signed by the person responsible for each entry.

The birth notification form is completed immediately after birth and submitted to the civil registration system to register the birth as a live birth. Timely birth registration is the foundation for the child's future right to education, healthcare, and legal identity. In India, the Births and Deaths Registration Act requires registration within twenty-one days of birth. Parents should be given clear guidance on how to complete this registration and what documents are needed.

The newborn health record, including the birth weight, Apgar scores, any resuscitation, medicines given, and initial examination findings, initiates the baby's lifelong health record. This record follows the child through immunizations, developmental assessments, and health check-ups.

The mother's postnatal notes document her condition after delivery, the findings of postnatal examinations, the medicines prescribed, and the contraception discussion. These notes inform the community health worker or primary care team who will follow up the mother after discharge.

Discharge documentation for both mother and baby should include clear written instructions about warning signs requiring urgent return, the schedule of follow-up appointments, feeding guidance, and contact information. Verbal instructions alone are insufficient. Written documentation that the mother takes home is her safety net in the critical days after discharge.

Part V: Mother's Recovery After Birth

Chapter 138: Ongoing Care of the Mother After Delivery

My dear,

Delivery is not the end of the journey. For the mother, it is the beginning of a new and equally important chapter. The weeks after birth are a time when the body is working hard to heal, the hormones are shifting dramatically, and a completely new life of mothering is beginning all at once. This period needs as much careful attention as pregnancy itself.

In the hours after delivery, the womb begins to contract back to its original size. This process can cause cramping that feels similar to labour pains, particularly when the baby feeds. These cramps are a healthy sign that the womb is doing its important work. Bleeding called lochia continues for several days to weeks after birth. It starts red and heavy, gradually becomes lighter, and changes to a pale yellowish colour before stopping. This is a normal part of recovery.

The mother's blood pressure, temperature, pulse, and bleeding are all checked regularly in the first day after birth. If any of these become abnormal, it may signal a complication such as infection or excessive blood loss, and prompt care is needed. Do not dismiss fever, very heavy bleeding, severe pain, or feeling faint after delivery as normal tiredness.

The mother needs to rest as much as the newborn allows. Sleep deprivation in the early days after birth is one of the hardest parts of recovery. Whenever the baby sleeps, the mother should also rest rather than using that time for household tasks. Family support in these first days is not a luxury. It is a genuine medical need.

Eating warm, nourishing food and drinking plenty of water supports healing, milk production, and emotional recovery. A mother who is well cared for by those around her recovers faster and breastfeeds more successfully.

Chapter 139: The Normal Recovery Period After Birth

My dear,

Every mother heals at her own pace after birth. Some feel remarkably strong within a day or two, while others need several weeks before they feel like themselves again. Both are within the range of normal. Recovery is shaped by the type of delivery, the length of labour, any complications, the mother's overall health, her nutrition, and the support she receives at home.

For a mother who delivered vaginally without any tearing, physical recovery is generally faster. The area below may feel tender and swollen for a few days. A small amount of discomfort during sitting is common. Pouring warm water while passing urine helps reduce stinging. Ice packs wrapped in cloth, applied gently to the tender area, reduce swelling in the first day or two.

For a mother who had a caesarean section, the recovery involves healing from major abdominal surgery. The cut in the abdomen heals in layers, and the skin wound usually closes within a week, but internal healing continues for six weeks or more. Pain at the cut site, some difficulty moving, and tiredness are all expected. Gentle movement is encouraged to prevent clots in the legs, but heavy lifting and vigorous activity must be avoided.

Whether the delivery was vaginal or surgical, the mother should avoid cold water baths, heavy physical work, lifting heavy objects, and sexual activity until her six-week check confirms that healing is complete. These are not old-fashioned customs. They are practical, evidence-based protections for the healing body.

Signs that recovery is not going normally include fever above thirty-eight degrees, foul-smelling discharge, increasing pain rather than decreasing pain, redness or pus at a wound site, or difficulty breathing. Any of these need immediate medical attention.

Chapter 140: Checking and Caring for the Mother at Home and Center

My dear,

After leaving the hospital or birth centre, the mother continues to need regular checking even in the comfort of her home. The transition from the monitored environment of a birth facility to the home setting is a vulnerable time. Problems can develop quietly, and without regular checking, they may not be noticed until they become serious.

A trained health worker or midwife should ideally visit the home within the first forty-eight hours of discharge. During this visit, the mother's bleeding is checked. Heavy bleeding, passage of large clots, or bleeding that is increasing rather than decreasing needs urgent attention. The womb should feel firm when pressed gently on the lower abdomen. A soft, tender, or painful womb after the first day may indicate retained placenta or infection.

The mother's temperature is checked. Even a low-grade fever after birth deserves attention, as infection of the womb lining, called endometritis, is a serious complication of delivery that can escalate quickly if untreated. The breasts are examined to assess whether milk has come in and whether the baby is latching and feeding well. Engorged, hard, or painful breasts need early support to prevent mastitis.

The perineal area or the caesarean wound is inspected for healing. A healthy wound shows gradual closing of the edges, no redness spreading beyond the wound edges, and no discharge other than clear serum in the first couple of days. Any gap opening in the wound, increasing redness, or pus formation needs immediate review.

At the health centre follow-up visit, typically at one week and six weeks after delivery, blood pressure, anaemia, emotional wellbeing, and contraception plans are also discussed. These visits are not just routine. They are an important safety net for the mother's health.

Chapter 141: Cleanliness and Care of the Tender Area Below

My dear,

The area between the legs deserves gentle, consistent care in the days and weeks after a vaginal delivery. Whether or not there was a tear or an episiotomy, this area has been through significant pressure and stretching. Keeping it clean and comfortable supports healing and prevents infection.

Washing the area gently with clean warm water after every time the toilet is used is the most important care step. Soap can be used sparingly but should not be strongly perfumed or antibacterial, as these can disrupt the natural healing environment. Patting the area dry gently with a clean cloth rather than rubbing is important. Rubbing causes friction on healing tissue.

Sanitary pads should be changed regularly, ideally every four to six hours or whenever they become soaked, even in the first heavy days. Letting a soaked pad sit against the healing skin increases the risk of infection. Hands should be washed carefully before and after changing pads. This small habit prevents many infections.

If stitches were placed after a tear or episiotomy, they usually dissolve on their own within two to three weeks. The stitched area may feel tight, itchy, or sore as it heals. This is normal. Sitting on a soft cushion or using a rolled cloth for support can make sitting more comfortable during this time.

Signs that the stitched area is not healing normally include increasing pain after the first few days, a bad smell, discharge that is yellow or green, a visible gap in the stitches, or significant swelling with redness. If any of these are noticed, medical review should not be delayed.

Sitz baths, where the woman sits in a shallow basin of clean warm water for ten to fifteen minutes, can provide significant relief from discomfort and promote healing. This can be done two to three times daily in the first week.

Chapter 142: Passing Urine and Stool Comfortably After Birth

My dear,

Passing urine and stool in the first days after birth can feel more difficult than expected. For the mother who has just delivered, the muscles of the pelvic floor have been stretched considerably. The bladder and bowel, which sit very close to the womb and vagina, have also been under significant pressure during labour. Some temporary difficulty is completely normal and expected.

Passing urine is usually easier to re-establish. Most women pass urine within six hours of a vaginal delivery. However, some women feel a burning or stinging sensation, particularly if there are stitches nearby. Pouring a steady stream of clean warm water over the area while urinating significantly reduces this discomfort. This simple method works remarkably well and requires no special equipment.

If urine cannot be passed at all within six to eight hours of delivery, this is important information for the midwife or doctor. The bladder can become overfull without the mother feeling the usual urge to urinate, particularly after epidural pain relief. An overfull bladder is both uncomfortable and can interfere with womb contraction. A catheter may be needed briefly to drain it.

Passing stool for the first time after birth is often dreaded. The fear of pain, particularly near stitches, causes many women to hold back. This unfortunately makes things worse, as the stool becomes harder and more difficult to pass with delay. Drinking plenty of water, eating fibre-rich foods including vegetables and fruits, and gentle movement all help to keep the stool soft and easy to pass.

A mild stool softener prescribed by the doctor or midwife is very helpful in the first week after delivery, particularly after a caesarean. This is not a strong laxative. It simply prevents the stool from hardening during the recovery period.

Chapter 143: Small Problems After Birth and Their Care

My dear,

After delivery, the mother may notice several small but uncomfortable problems that are not dangerous but do need attention and care. Understanding these in advance helps the mother recognise them quickly and manage them without anxiety.

Afterpains are cramps in the lower abdomen that occur as the womb contracts back to its pre-pregnancy size. These are felt more strongly during breastfeeding because the hormone oxytocin, released during feeding, causes the womb to contract. They are usually more noticeable with second and subsequent pregnancies and tend to lessen after the first two to three days. Paracetamol at the recommended dose provides good relief.

Haemorrhoids, which are swollen veins around the back passage, often develop during pregnancy and may worsen during the pushing stage of labour. They cause itching, discomfort, and sometimes bleeding when stools are passed. Keeping stools soft, avoiding prolonged sitting on the toilet, and using prescribed creams or suppositories as directed all help. They usually resolve within a few weeks.

Breast engorgement occurs when the milk comes in, typically between the second and fifth day after birth. The breasts feel hard, heavy, and warm. Feeding the baby frequently, using warm compresses before feeding, and expressing a small amount of milk to soften the areola before latching all reduce engorgement and help the baby feed more easily.

Night sweats are very common in the first week after birth. The body is releasing the extra fluid accumulated during pregnancy, and hormonal changes cause significant sweating, particularly at night. This is not fever. It resolves on its own within a week or two.

Fatigue is perhaps the most universal small problem after birth. Rest whenever possible, accept help from family, and do not expect to function at full capacity in the first weeks.

Chapter 144: How Milk Starts and How Feeding Gets Established

My dear,

Breast milk does not appear immediately after birth. What the baby receives in the first two to three days is a special early fluid called colostrum. Colostrum is thick, yellowish, and produced in small but concentrated amounts. It is exactly what a newborn needs. It is rich in antibodies, proteins, and growth factors. Every small drop of colostrum is valuable. It coats the inside of the baby's gut and offers powerful protection against infection.

The mother's mature milk usually comes in between the second and fifth day after birth. This transition is often felt as a sudden fullness, heaviness, and warmth in the breasts. Some mothers feel a tingling sensation, particularly when the baby begins to feed. This let-down reflex shows that milk is flowing.

Milk production works on the principle of supply and demand. The more the baby feeds, the more milk the body produces. Restricting feeds or giving supplemental feeds of water, sugar water, or formula in the early days significantly reduces the stimulus to the breast and can interfere with establishing a good milk supply. Unless medically necessary, these supplements are not recommended in the first weeks.

The baby should be offered the breast eight to twelve times in twenty-four hours in the early days. This frequent feeding pattern is normal and expected. It does not mean that the milk supply is insufficient. Newborns have small stomachs and digest breast milk quickly, so they genuinely need to feed often.

Signs that feeding is going well include the baby latching without painful nipple damage, audible swallowing during feeds, at least six wet nappies per day from day four onwards, and steady weight gain after the initial loss in the first few days. A lactation counsellor can provide invaluable support if any of these signs are absent.

Chapter 145: Counseling and Emotional Support After Delivery

My dear,

The emotional experience of becoming a mother is profound, complex, and often surprising. Many women expect to feel immediate, overwhelming joy after birth. When the actual emotions are more complicated than this, it can feel confusing or even shameful. Emotional support after delivery is just as important as physical care, and it deserves the same serious attention.

A warm, reassuring conversation from a midwife, doctor, or counsellor in the days after birth can make a significant difference to how a mother experiences the beginning of her mothering journey. Being told honestly that mixed feelings, moments of doubt, exhaustion, and overwhelm are completely normal reduces the sense of isolation that many new mothers quietly carry.

The partner and immediate family play a critical role in emotional support. A mother who feels seen, appreciated, and practically supported is significantly less likely to struggle with her emotional recovery. Simple acts carry enormous weight: bringing warm food, sitting beside her while she feeds, taking the baby for a short time so she can sleep, and saying sincerely that she is doing well.

Listening to a new mother is one of the most powerful forms of support. When she speaks about difficulties, the response should never be to immediately offer solutions, dismiss concerns, or compare her experience unfavourably to others. She needs to feel that her experience is real and valued.

Counselling sessions, whether formal or through trusted conversations, should address feeding challenges, the adjustment of identity, changes in the relationship with the partner, and fears about the baby's wellbeing. These are genuine concerns that deserve genuine responses, not quick reassurance.

Every new mother deserves to be surrounded by kindness. She has done something extraordinary, and the care she receives in the weeks that follow will shape her experience of motherhood for a very long time.

Chapter 146: Baby Blues and Deeper Sadness After Birth

My dear,

In the days following delivery, many mothers experience a period of emotional vulnerability that is so common it has its own name: the baby blues. As many as eight in ten new mothers experience it. It typically begins between the second and fifth day after birth, when hormones are shifting rapidly, and usually resolves within a week or two without treatment.

The baby blues can feel like sudden sadness without a clear reason, tearfulness, irritability, anxiety, difficulty sleeping even when the baby is sleeping, and a sense of being overwhelmed. These feelings arrive at a time when the mother expected to feel happy, which makes them more confusing. Understanding that these feelings are driven by the dramatic hormonal changes of the post-delivery period, not by personal weakness or failure as a mother, is genuinely helpful.

The baby blues are supported by rest, kind company, reassurance, and practical help. They do not usually require medication. They pass.

Postpartum depression is different. It is more persistent, more intense, and does not resolve on its own without support or treatment. Postpartum depression affects roughly one in eight new mothers and can develop any time in the first year after birth, though it most often becomes apparent in the first few months.

Signs of postpartum depression include persistent sadness or emptiness lasting more than two weeks, inability to feel pleasure in anything including the baby, extreme anxiety or panic, strong feelings of worthlessness or guilt, difficulty bonding with the baby, frightening thoughts, withdrawal from family and friends, and difficulty caring for the baby or oneself.

Postpartum depression is not a personal failing. It is a medical condition that responds well to appropriate support, counselling, and sometimes medication. Seeking help is a sign of strength, not weakness. The mother who gets help recovers and thrives.

Chapter 147: Growing Into Motherhood and Fatherhood

My dear,

Becoming a parent is not a single moment. It is a gradual process of growing into an entirely new identity while still being the same person. The transition into motherhood and fatherhood deserves patience, understanding, and the freedom to unfold at its own pace.

For the mother, everything changes at once. Her body is recovering from the enormous effort of pregnancy and delivery. Her sleep is fragmented in ways that affect thinking, emotions, and physical resilience. Her sense of self has shifted. She is someone's mother now, and figuring out what that means alongside who she already was takes time.

Many new mothers describe a period of intense focus on the baby that leaves them feeling as though they have lost themselves. This is a normal and temporary adjustment. The self does not disappear. It expands, slowly and often beautifully, to hold this new dimension. But the process can be disorienting in the early weeks.

For the new father, the transition also involves significant adjustment that is less visible and often less supported. He has watched the birth, carried a worry about the safety of his partner and baby through the whole pregnancy, and is now expected to take on the role of father without much preparation. He may feel uncertain about how to help, left on the edges of the intense mother-baby pair, and unsure of his place in this new configuration of the family.

Couples who talk honestly about these feelings, who acknowledge that they are both adjusting, and who make small gestures of care toward one another alongside caring for the baby, find the transition significantly more manageable. The arrival of a baby is the beginning of a family. Growing into that family is the beautiful, imperfect, genuine work of new parenthood.

Chapter 148: Caring for the Mother Up to Six Weeks

My dear,

The six-week period after delivery is formally called the puerperium. It is the time during which the body gradually returns to its pre-pregnancy state. Most of the dramatic changes that pregnancy brought, from the enlarged womb to the increased blood volume to the altered hormonal environment, reverse during this period. Understanding what this involves helps the mother navigate it with realistic expectations.

In the first week, the priority is rest, healing, and establishing feeding. The mother should not be expected to manage the household, entertain visitors, or return to any kind of normal activity. Her one job is to recover and to learn her baby.

In the second and third weeks, healing continues. Fatigue remains significant. The mother may begin to feel slightly more herself, and the feeding relationship with the baby usually becomes more comfortable during this time.

By the fourth to sixth week, most physical healing is complete for an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. For caesarean delivery, internal healing continues longer, though the external wound is usually well-healed. Energy begins to return gradually, though full energy often takes several more weeks.

The six-week check-up is an important milestone. At this visit, the womb is examined to confirm it has returned to its normal size and position. Blood pressure, anaemia, and wound healing are assessed. Emotional wellbeing is discussed. Contraception options are reviewed and a decision made based on individual circumstances. For mothers who have not yet begun reliable contraception, it is important to know that ovulation can return before the first period after birth.

The six-week check is also an opportunity to raise any concerns that have been accumulating, whether physical, emotional, or about feeding and infant care. This visit belongs entirely to the mother.

Chapter 149: Food Beliefs After Birth: What Helps and What Harms

My dear,

In almost every culture across India and beyond, new mothers are given specific food instructions in the weeks after delivery. Some of these traditional recommendations are genuinely supportive of recovery. Others are restrictions that can, if followed too strictly, actually harm the recovering mother by limiting the nutrients she needs most.

Warm foods are generally beneficial after delivery. They support digestion, provide comfort, and are easier for the recovering body to process. Many traditional foods given after birth, such as ghee with rice, fenugreek laddoos, dry fruit preparations, and warm soups with lentils, are nutritionally excellent. They provide iron, healthy fats, protein, and energy at a time when all of these are needed in abundance.

The restrictions deserve more careful consideration. In some communities, new mothers are told to avoid raw vegetables, fruits, water, most pulses, and any cooling foods. These restrictions, if followed strictly, can lead to significant constipation, dehydration, and nutritional gaps that delay recovery and reduce milk production.

A new mother needs approximately five hundred extra calories per day above her usual needs while breastfeeding, along with generous amounts of fluid, iron-rich foods to recover from blood loss, calcium-rich foods to support milk production, and protein to rebuild the tissues of recovery.

Encouraging the new mother to eat a wide variety of warm, nourishing, home-cooked foods and to drink plenty of water, warm soups, and milk is far more beneficial than a restrictive list of forbidden foods. If a cultural restriction feels important to follow, it is always worth discussing it with a doctor or nutritionist to understand whether it can be balanced without compromising recovery.

The new mother's body has done enormous work. It deserves abundant, nourishing food, offered with warmth and love.

Chapter 150: Food During Breastfeeding

My dear,

A breastfeeding mother needs more energy, more fluid, and more of several specific nutrients than she needs at any other point in her life outside of pregnancy. What she eats directly affects her own recovery, her milk supply, and through her milk, the nutritional quality available to her growing baby.

Calories come first. A breastfeeding mother needs approximately four hundred to five hundred extra calories each day above her pre-pregnancy intake. This is not the time for dieting or calorie restriction. Even mothers who want to manage their post-birth weight should wait until breastfeeding is well established, and any weight management approach should be gentle and supervised, not restrictive.

Iron is a priority after birth because delivery involves blood loss. Iron-rich foods include dark green leafy vegetables such as spinach and fenugreek, lentils, chickpeas, kidney beans, eggs, and if non-vegetarian, red meat. Consuming these alongside a source of vitamin C significantly improves iron absorption.

Calcium supports milk production and also protects the mother's own bone health, since breastfeeding draws on calcium reserves. Dairy products, ragi, sesame seeds, almonds, and calcium-set tofu are good sources.

Fluid intake is one of the most important factors in maintaining milk supply. The mother should drink water, warm soups, herbal teas, and milk throughout the day. A practical approach is to drink a full glass of water each time the baby is put to the breast.

A few foods are known to potentially cause wind or discomfort in some babies, including very spicy food and excess caffeine. However, most healthy foods are perfectly safe during breastfeeding. There is no need to eat a plain or limited diet. A varied, nutritious, well-hydrated diet is the best diet for a breastfeeding mother and her baby.

Chapter 151: Family Planning After Delivery

My dear,

One of the most important conversations after delivery is about family planning. Although the body has just completed a pregnancy, the possibility of another pregnancy returning sooner than expected is real. Many women are surprised to learn that ovulation can return before the first period after delivery. This means that pregnancy is possible before any visible sign of the monthly cycle returning.

For exclusively breastfeeding mothers, the lactational amenorrhoea method offers some natural protection against pregnancy in the first six months after birth, provided the baby is fed at least every four hours during the day and every six hours at night without any supplements. Even with this method, the protection is not absolute, and it reduces significantly once the baby begins receiving other foods or feeds less frequently.

Family planning options suitable for use after delivery include barrier methods such as condoms, which can be started immediately. Progestogen-only hormonal methods, including the mini-pill, the hormonal injection, and the hormonal implant, are compatible with breastfeeding and can be started within the first few weeks after delivery. The copper intrauterine device can be placed within forty-eight hours of delivery or after six weeks.

Combined oral contraceptive pills containing both oestrogen and progesterone are generally not recommended in the first six months for breastfeeding mothers, as oestrogen can reduce milk supply.

Emergency contraception remains available for use after unprotected intercourse.

The right family planning method is the one that fits the mother's health, feeding plans, future pregnancy wishes, and personal preference. A calm, non-pressured discussion with a health provider helps each woman choose what is right for her specific situation. Family planning is an act of care, not only for the woman herself, but for her current baby and her family's future.

Chapter 152: Follow-Up Visits After Delivery

My dear,

Follow-up visits after delivery are not optional extras. They are an essential part of safe motherhood care, designed to catch complications early, support recovery, and ensure that the mother and baby are both thriving in the weeks after leaving the birth facility.

The recommended visits after a normal delivery include a check within twenty-four to forty-eight hours after going home, particularly important when hospital discharge happens early. A check at one week after delivery assesses wound healing, feeding progress, emotional wellbeing, and any physical concerns. The most important follow-up is at six weeks, when a comprehensive examination of the mother's physical recovery, her emotional health, her baby's growth, and her family planning needs are all addressed.

For mothers who had a caesarean delivery, additional visits may be recommended for wound assessment, and the return to normal activity is guided by how healing progresses at these visits.

At each follow-up visit, the mother should feel free to raise any concern, however small it may seem. Questions about feeding, changes in the baby's feeding or sleeping pattern, discomfort or unusual physical symptoms, mood difficulties, relationship adjustments, and family planning are all appropriate topics. No question is too minor.

Before leaving each visit, the mother should clearly understand when and where to seek help urgently if a problem develops between planned visits. She should know the warning signs of serious complications such as heavy bleeding, fever, signs of infection, chest pain, or severe headache.

Community health workers, ASHA workers, and ANMs play a vital role in home visits during this period in India, bringing care directly to the mother when travelling is difficult. Their visits are part of a complete system of care, not just a formality. Each visit is an opportunity to strengthen health, resolve concerns, and move forward with confidence.

Chapter 153: Medicines Used After Delivery

My dear,

Several medicines are routinely used in the period immediately after delivery and in the weeks of recovery. Understanding why these are given and how to take them safely helps the mother use them effectively and reduces the chance of missing important doses.

Oxytocin is the most important medicine used immediately after delivery. It is given by injection, usually into the upper thigh or a vein, within one minute of the baby being born. Its purpose is to cause the womb to contract firmly, which pushes the placenta out and controls bleeding. This single medicine prevents a large proportion of postpartum haemorrhage deaths worldwide.

Iron and folic acid tablets are continued after delivery because of the blood loss of delivery and the additional demands of breastfeeding. Iron tablets are best absorbed when taken on an empty stomach or with a small glass of orange juice. They commonly cause dark-coloured stools, which is harmless, and can cause some nausea or constipation. Taking them with food reduces nausea but also reduces absorption slightly.

Calcium tablets support the mother's own bone health during breastfeeding and are often continued in the postpartum period.

Paracetamol is the safest pain relief option for the breastfeeding mother. It passes into breast milk only in very small amounts and is considered safe for the feeding baby. It effectively manages afterpains, wound discomfort, and general postpartum pain.

Antibiotics may be prescribed after a caesarean delivery or after a tear with significant risk of infection. It is important to complete the full course as prescribed, even if the wound appears to be healing well before the course finishes.

No medicine, including herbal preparations, should be started during breastfeeding without checking with a doctor or pharmacist that it is safe. When in doubt, always ask before taking anything.

Chapter 154: Good Records and Reports After Birth

My dear,

Good documentation after birth matters more than many families realise. Clear, accurate records of the delivery, the newborn's examination findings, and the mother's recovery protect both mother and baby if any concern arises in the weeks and months ahead. They also form the foundation of future healthcare decisions.

The hospital or birth centre should provide a discharge summary that includes the date and type of delivery, the baby's birth weight, the Apgar score, any complications during delivery or immediately after, medicines given to the mother or baby, and instructions for follow-up care. This document should be kept safely and brought to every future healthcare visit.

The baby's health card or child health record begins at birth and must be maintained carefully. It records birth weight, all immunisations with dates and batch numbers, growth measurements at each visit, developmental milestones, and any illnesses or treatments. This document travels with the child throughout childhood and forms the basis of school health records and future medical care.

The mother's own healthcare record should document her delivery details, her blood type and Rh factor, any complications, medicines used, and follow-up visit findings. If the mother has a condition such as gestational diabetes, hypertension of pregnancy, or anaemia, this must be clearly recorded for future reference, as these conditions carry implications for long-term health.

In an emergency, a clear record in hand can save valuable time. A healthcare provider seeing a patient for the first time in an emergency setting can act immediately and appropriately when a clear discharge summary is available.

Every piece of paper from the birth facility deserves to be kept carefully in one place, ideally in a plastic sleeve or folder that can be easily taken to appointments. A family that keeps good records is a family that receives better care at every visit.

Part VI: Newborn Care

Chapter 155: Regular Care of a Healthy Newborn

My dear,

A healthy newborn needs a small number of consistently provided essentials: warmth, feeding, cleanliness, safety, and love. When these are provided reliably, most healthy babies grow and thrive without requiring much else in the first weeks of life.

Warmth is the first priority. Newborns cannot regulate their own body temperature effectively. They lose heat quickly, particularly through the head. Keeping the baby dressed in appropriate layers, with the head covered when in a cool environment, and avoiding cold rooms and fans directed at the baby is important. A simple test of the baby's warmth is to check the chest or back of the neck. It should feel warm to the touch, not cold or clammy.

Feeding is the second priority, and for most newborns, this means breast milk. The baby should be offered the breast at the first sign of hunger, which often appears as turning the head from side to side, opening the mouth, or bringing the hands to the face. Crying is a late hunger sign. Waiting for crying before feeding makes latching more difficult.

Cleanliness involves keeping the navel stump clean and dry until it falls off naturally, usually within one to three weeks. The baby's eyes, face, and nappy area are cleaned gently with clean water on a soft cloth.

Safety means never leaving the baby unattended on a raised surface, always supporting the baby's head when carrying, avoiding sleeping in the same bed with the baby if the parent is very tired, and keeping the baby away from cigarette smoke and strong chemicals.

Love means speaking softly, responding to cries, holding and carrying the baby, making gentle eye contact, and creating a calm, consistent environment. The baby learns that the world is a safe place through every consistent, kind response it receives. This learning is the foundation of all future emotional security.

Chapter 156: Caring for the Baby with the Family

My dear,

A newborn does not belong only to the mother. A newborn joins a family. How the whole family participates in the care of a new baby shapes both the baby's early experience and the wellbeing of every person in the household. Shared care distributes the enormous work of a newborn, strengthens the bonds between the baby and the wider family, and significantly reduces the burden on the mother during her recovery.

The father plays a unique and irreplaceable role in newborn care that begins from the first hours of life. Skin-to-skin contact with the father, where the naked baby is held against the father's bare chest and covered with a warm blanket, is calming for the baby, promotes bonding, and gives the mother a period of rest. Fathers who are included in feeding, bathing, nappy changing, and settling routines from the very beginning develop a confident, close relationship with their baby.

Grandparents, where they are present and willing, bring a wealth of experience and a depth of love that is genuinely valuable. However, their involvement is most helpful when it is guided by current evidence-based practices alongside their tradition and experience.

Older siblings may feel confused, displaced, or even resentful when a new baby arrives. Acknowledging their feelings, involving them in small caring tasks appropriate to their age, and ensuring they still receive dedicated attention from their parents helps manage this transition. Children who feel included rather than replaced adjust to a new sibling much more successfully.

When the whole family cares for a new baby together, with shared responsibility and mutual support, the baby thrives and every member of the family grows. A baby is not a burden on a family. A baby is the newest member of a community of people who will love and protect this child for a lifetime.

Chapter 157: Respectful Care and Kind Speech for the Newborn

My dear,

The way a newborn is spoken to, held, and handled in the very first weeks of life matters more than most families realise. Babies are not blank receivers of physical care. From birth, they are social beings. They recognise their mother's voice, which they have been hearing since before twenty-eight weeks of pregnancy. They respond to tone, warmth, and calmness in the voices around them.

Respectful care means handling the baby gently and with intention. Sudden movements, loud noises, and rough handling startle the newborn's immature nervous system. Startling repeatedly and without comfort creates a state of low-level stress in the baby that affects sleep, feeding, and settling. Gentle, predictable movements, slow transitions from one position to another, and speaking softly before touching the baby all reduce startling and promote calmness.

Kind speech is not about talking constantly. It is about the quality of how the baby is spoken to. When the baby is picked up, saying something simple and warm tells the baby that it is safe and loved. Studies consistently show that babies who are spoken to warmly and frequently from birth develop language skills earlier and more fully.

Eye contact during feeding, during settling, and during quiet awake periods is a powerful form of connection. Looking into a newborn's eyes and speaking softly communicates safety and love in a way the baby genuinely receives.

Responding to a baby's cry is not spoiling the baby. It is building the foundation of trust. A baby whose cries are consistently met with a warm, reliable response learns that the world is safe and that communication has meaning. This learning is the very beginning of emotional intelligence, language development, and secure attachment that will shape the child's relationships for the rest of its life.

Chapter 158: How a Newborn Adjusts After Birth

My dear,

Birth is the most dramatic environmental change a human being ever experiences. In the space of minutes, the baby moves from the warm, muffled, fluid-filled world of the womb into a bright, loud, cool, air-filled world that requires entirely new ways of breathing, feeding, maintaining temperature, and processing sensation. The newborn's body is remarkably prepared for this transition, but it still requires time and support to complete the adjustment.

The first breath after birth is the most important breath the baby will ever take. Air enters the lungs for the first time, collapsing the fluid that filled them and establishing the pattern of breathing that will sustain life. Most babies take their first breath within the first minute. Crying is one way the baby opens the airways fully, and the sound of a newborn crying at birth is therefore one of the most reassuring sounds in a delivery room.

The circulation of blood changes at birth. In the womb, the placenta does the work of the lungs. At birth, the vessels that allowed blood to bypass the lungs must close as the lungs take over. This process takes a few hours to days to complete. During this transition, the baby may look slightly blue around the lips or hands, which is normal. However, persistent blueness of the face, tongue, or trunk needs immediate assessment.

The newborn's digestive system must begin its work for the first time. The first stool, called meconium, is dark greenish-black, sticky, and odourless. It is the accumulated waste products of the months in the womb. It usually passes within the first twenty-four to forty-eight hours, and feeding helps to move it through.

Temperature regulation, blood sugar stability, and the transition between sleep and wakeful states all occur in these first hours and days. Support from warmth, skin-to-skin contact, and early feeding makes each of these adjustments smoother.
