Chapter 159: Checking the Newborn and Looking for Birth Problems

My dear,

Every newborn receives a careful examination in the first hours after birth. This examination is not a formality. It is a systematic search for conditions that need early identification and care. Many birth-related problems respond very well to early treatment and have poor outcomes when found late.

The Apgar score, recorded at one minute and five minutes after birth, is a quick assessment of five signs: the baby's colour, heart rate, reflexes, muscle tone, and breathing. Each sign is scored from zero to two, giving a maximum total of ten. A score between seven and ten at five minutes is normal and reassuring. A lower score at five minutes prompts additional support and close monitoring.

The physical examination after birth includes checking the baby's head carefully for any moulding from passage through the birth canal, which is normal and resolves within days. The fontanelle, the soft spot on the top of the head, should be flat, not bulging or sunken. The palate is checked for any gap. The eyes are examined for signs of infection or abnormal structure.

The heart and lungs are listened to with a stethoscope. An abnormal heart sound called a murmur may indicate a heart problem, though many murmurs in newborns are innocent and resolve on their own. The abdomen is palpated for normal organ sizes.

The spine is examined for any skin dimple, hair tuft, or swelling along its length. The hips are gently manipulated to check for proper joint formation. All limbs are counted and checked for normal structure and movement.

Any concern found at this examination is discussed with the family clearly and honestly. Early identification of a problem is always better than late discovery. Parents should feel free to ask questions during this examination and to ask for a clear explanation of any finding that concerns them.

Chapter 160: Routine Care of the Baby in the First Six Weeks

My dear,

The first six weeks of a baby's life is a period of rapid change and gradual adjustment. For parents, it is a time of learning the language of this specific baby: what each type of cry means, how the baby likes to be held, what settles them, and how their sleep and feeding patterns begin to emerge.

Weight is an important marker of how well the baby is doing. Most babies lose up to seven percent of their birth weight in the first few days as they pass meconium and adjust to feeding. This is normal. The birth weight should be regained by ten to fourteen days. After that, a healthy weight gain of approximately one hundred and fifty to two hundred grams per week is expected. Persistent weight loss or failure to regain birth weight by two weeks needs urgent assessment.

Umbilical cord care continues until the stump falls off, usually between one and three weeks. Keeping it dry and clean, folding the nappy below it to allow air circulation, and not applying powders or oils to it supports natural separation.

The baby's eyes may produce a small amount of clear discharge in the first week, which is cleaned gently with a clean cotton ball moistened with clean water, wiping from the inner corner outward. Yellow or green sticky discharge from the eyes needs assessment for infection.

The bath in the first weeks should be a gentle, warm sponge bath with minimal soap, with special care taken to keep the navel stump dry. A full immersion bath is introduced after the cord stump has fallen and the navel area is completely healed.

Development in the first six weeks includes the baby beginning to track movement with the eyes, showing a social smile typically from around four to six weeks, and responding with increased alertness to familiar voices. Every small milestone is worth noticing and celebrating.

Chapter 161: Skin-to-Skin Care and Keeping the Baby Warm

My dear,

Skin-to-skin care, the practice of placing a naked or lightly clothed baby directly against the bare chest of the mother or father, is one of the most powerful and most accessible forms of newborn care available. It requires no equipment, no medication, and no special skill. It simply requires the willingness to hold the baby close.

The benefits of skin-to-skin care are supported by decades of research. For the baby, it stabilises body temperature, blood sugar, heart rate, and breathing more effectively than any incubator device in the immediate newborn period. It supports the establishment of breastfeeding by positioning the baby near the breast and triggering the natural feeding reflexes. It reduces the baby's experience of pain during uncomfortable procedures. It promotes early and deep bonding.

For the mother, skin-to-skin contact after delivery promotes the release of oxytocin, the bonding hormone, which helps the womb contract and reduces postpartum blood loss. It supports milk production and the let-down reflex. It reduces postpartum anxiety and promotes a sense of connection with the baby.

For preterm or low birth weight babies, skin-to-skin care is called kangaroo mother care and has been shown to significantly improve survival rates, reduce infection, and shorten the time needed in hospital. Even brief periods of kangaroo care, done as often as possible, produce measurable benefits.

Keeping a newborn warm through all care activities is essential. Bathing, weighing, and examining the baby should all be done in a warm environment and completed quickly to minimise heat loss. A baby who becomes cold uses valuable energy warming up rather than growing.

The single most important thing that every person caring for a newborn can do is simple: hold the baby close, keep the baby warm, and respond to the baby's signals with consistent, gentle care.

Chapter 162: Preventing Infection in the Newborn

My dear,

Newborns have immature immune systems. They are born with some antibody protection passed from the mother through the placenta during pregnancy, and they receive further antibodies through colostrum and breast milk. But their own immune response to infection is still developing, and they are genuinely vulnerable to bacteria, viruses, and fungi that a healthy older child or adult would handle without difficulty.

Preventing infection in the newborn is therefore one of the most important responsibilities of everyone who cares for the baby. Handwashing is the single most effective infection prevention measure available. Every person who touches the baby, including parents, grandparents, siblings, health workers, and visitors, should wash their hands with soap and water for at least twenty seconds before touching the baby. This single habit prevents the majority of newborn infections.

Visitors who have respiratory infections, fever, vomiting, diarrhoea, or active cold sores should not hold or handle the baby. In the first two months of life, any infection in a newborn is a potential medical emergency and must be assessed by a doctor.

The navel area should be kept clean and dry and not covered with cloth that traps moisture. Infection at the navel, which enters through the umbilical stump before it is fully sealed, can track rapidly into the bloodstream and cause serious illness.

Breastfeeding provides significant protection against intestinal infections by providing antibodies, probiotics, and immune-active substances directly to the baby's gut with every feed. A baby who is exclusively breastfed has dramatically lower rates of gastroenteritis, respiratory infections, and ear infections than a baby who is fed formula.

Clean surroundings, clean hands, and clean equipment used in the baby's care are the practical foundations of infection prevention. These are not difficult measures. They are consistent ones.

Chapter 163: Protective Injections for the Baby

My dear,

Vaccination is one of the most important gifts parents can give their child. The immunisations given in infancy and childhood protect against diseases that once killed or permanently disabled millions of children every year. These diseases have not disappeared from the world. They exist and circulate, and vaccination keeps the protection active.

In India, the Universal Immunisation Programme provides free vaccinations to all children from birth. The schedule begins at birth with the BCG vaccine, which provides protection against tuberculosis, and the first doses of the oral polio vaccine and hepatitis B vaccine. These are given within hours of birth at a hospital delivery or at the nearest health facility as soon as possible after a home delivery.

At six weeks, ten weeks, and fourteen weeks after birth, the baby receives a series of combination vaccines protecting against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, haemophilus influenzae type b, hepatitis B, polio, and pneumococcal disease. These are given as injections and drops together at each visit.

After each injection, a small amount of redness, swelling, and tenderness at the injection site is expected and normal. A mild fever in the twenty-four to forty-eight hours following vaccination is also a normal immune response. Paracetamol at the appropriate dose for the baby's weight helps manage this discomfort.

The vaccination card given at the first immunisation visit must be kept safely and brought to every subsequent vaccination. This card is the proof of the child's immunisation history and is required for school entry and other health assessments throughout childhood.

No vaccine in the standard immunisation schedule causes the diseases they protect against. The protection they offer is genuine, significant, and in many cases lifelong. Keeping to the schedule without delay gives the baby the strongest possible protection at the time when they are most vulnerable.

Chapter 164: Small Newborn Problems and Their Care

My dear,

Many newborns develop small problems in the first days and weeks of life that cause concern but are usually not dangerous and resolve without treatment or with simple care at home. Understanding which are normal and which are warning signs helps parents respond appropriately without either dismissing something important or worrying unnecessarily.

Newborn acne appears as small red or white spots on the baby's face, usually in the second to fourth week of life. It is caused by maternal hormones circulating in the baby's system and resolves on its own within a few weeks. It does not require treatment.

Milia are tiny white dots that appear most often on the nose, cheeks, and forehead of newborns. They are blocked skin glands. Like newborn acne, they resolve on their own without any treatment.

Cradle cap is a yellow, greasy, scaly patch that appears on the top of the baby's scalp. It is not an infection and is not harmful. Gently massaging a small amount of natural oil such as coconut oil onto the scalp, leaving it for a few minutes, and then combing gently with a soft comb often removes the scales gradually.

Hiccoughs are very common in newborns and are usually not distressing to the baby even when they appear prolonged. They resolve spontaneously.

Sneezing in newborns does not usually indicate a cold. Newborns sneeze frequently to clear their nasal passages. It is a normal reflex, not a sign of illness.

Sticky eyes are common and respond to gentle cleaning with clean water on cotton. Persistent stickiness or significant redness of the white of the eye needs medical assessment.

Any problem that is new, worsening, accompanied by fever, poor feeding, excessive crying, or changes in the baby's colour or breathing always warrants a medical assessment without delay.

Chapter 165: Family Welfare Services for the Whole Home

Family welfare services are one of the most valuable and most underused resources available to families in India and across many countries. These services exist to support not only the pregnant woman or the new mother, but the entire family unit: the baby, the children, the couple, and the household as a whole.

Family welfare services support women, babies, children, and the whole household through checkups, guidance, vaccinations, nutrition support, family planning advice, treatment referral, and warning-sign education. These services aim to keep families healthy before trouble grows. Using them early and regularly can prevent many serious problems later.

Protecting the mother is one of the best ways to protect the baby. A mother who receives consistent healthcare, emotional support, adequate nutrition, and respectful treatment is a mother who can care fully and confidently for her child. Family welfare services create the conditions in which this is possible.

At the primary health centre and community health centre level, these services include antenatal and postnatal care, child growth monitoring, immunisation programmes, nutritional supplementation such as iron, folic acid, and vitamin A, family planning services, and referral pathways to specialist care when needed.

Their home visits, their relationships with the families they serve, and their ability to identify early warning signs in both mother and child make them a critical part of the family welfare system.

Registering for care early in pregnancy, maintaining all follow-up visits, completing all vaccinations, and staying connected with the local health system through the postnatal period are the steps that make the difference between a family that manages difficulties as they arise and one that prevents them altogether. Early care protects both mother and baby at every stage.

Chapter 171: Emergency Protection After Unprotected Married Life

Chapter 174: Pregnancy Outside the Womb or Early Pregnancy Loss

My dear,

Sometimes the baby does not grow inside the womb. It may grow in a tube, called ectopic pregnancy, and this can become a life-threatening emergency. Sometimes pregnancy starts inside the womb but stops growing early, causing miscarriage. Warning signs are bleeding, one-sided pain, shoulder pain, fainting, passing clots, or strong cramps. Some light spotting can happen, but heavy bleeding or worsening pain must never be ignored. A urine test alone cannot tell where the pregnancy is. The doctor may need blood tests and ultrasound. Do not blame yourself. Many early losses happen because the pregnancy was not developing normally. Quick care matters because delay can harm the mother. Early bleeding with pain always deserves respect, fast attention, and medical review.

Chapter 175: Less Baby Movement and Labour Starting Too Early

My dear,

If your baby usually moves well but suddenly moves much less, do not wait till tomorrow. Eat, drink, lie quietly, and notice movements, but if the baby still seems quieter, call or go the same day. Reduced movement can be a warning sign. Labour starting before thirty-seven weeks is called preterm labour, meaning early labour. Warning signs include regular tightening, back pain, period-like cramps, pressure below, watery leaking, mucus discharge, or bleeding. These signs do not always mean birth will happen soon, but they must be checked. Early help can sometimes protect the baby and delay birth. Never feel foolish for reporting change. A mother noticing something different may help save her baby from danger by acting early.

Chapter 176: Cesarean Birth and Recovery

My dear,

A cesarean is an operation used when vaginal birth may not be safest for the mother, the baby, or both. It may be needed for heavy bleeding, placenta problems, labour not progressing, baby distress, breech position, or other medical reasons. A cesarean is not failure. It is another safe way to bring a baby into the world. Recovery is usually longer than after vaginal birth. The mother may have wound pain, tiredness, gas pain, and difficulty getting up at first. Early walking, good pain relief, help with feeding, clean wound care, and watching for fever, redness, swelling, or heavy bleeding are important. The mother also needs emotional support, because an operation can feel frightening. A safe mother and safe baby matter most.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 177: After Delivery: When to Call Urgently

My dear,

Many women think danger ends once the baby is born, but some serious problems begin later. Call urgently or go quickly if there is heavy bleeding soaking pads, very large clots, fainting, severe headache, blurred vision, chest pain, trouble breathing, one-leg swelling, fever, foul-smelling discharge, or severe belly pain. Also seek help if the mother feels deeply confused, cannot sleep at all, has frightening thoughts, or feels unable to care for herself or the baby. High blood pressure problems, blood clots, infection, and severe mental illness can happen after childbirth. The first days and weeks still need protection. Do not hide symptoms because visitors are home or the baby looks well. Fast action after birth can save life.

Chapter 178: Breastfeeding Problems and Breast Infection

My dear,

Many mothers want to feed well but face pain, fear, and confusion. Poor latch can cause sore nipples, cracked skin, and poor milk transfer. Hard swollen breasts may happen when milk builds up and does not drain well. A blocked duct may cause a tender lump. Mastitis means breast inflammation, often with fever, redness, and body ache, and sometimes needs medical treatment. Do not stop asking for help just because feeding is called natural. Early support matters. Good positioning, frequent feeding, emptying the breast well, rest, fluids, and checking the baby's latch can solve many problems. But fever, severe pain, spreading redness, or a very sleepy baby who is not feeding need quick review.

Chapter 179: Daily-Life Safety in Pregnancy

My dear,

Most women can continue many normal activities, but some habits need more care. Regular walking and safe exercise often help back pain, constipation, mood, and sleep. Heavy lifting, dangerous falls, overheating, and risky travel need caution. Travel is usually safe until close to the due date in healthy pregnancies, but bleeding, high blood pressure, twins, leaking waters, or early labour signs need medical advice first. Wear the seat belt low under the belly and across the shoulder, not over the bump. Sleep on the side later in pregnancy if comfortable. Sex is often safe unless the doctor advises against it because of bleeding, placenta problems, leaking, or early labour risk. Safe daily life means staying active wisely.

Chapter 180: Medicines, Herbs, and Self-Treatment Safety

My dear,

Never assume that a tablet, syrup, powder, herb, or home remedy is safe just because it is common, natural, or sold without prescription. Some medicines can affect the baby in the womb. Some medicines can pass into breast milk. Even painkillers, cold medicines, decongestants, and herbal mixtures may not be right for every mother. Also, do not stop important prescribed medicines suddenly without asking, because untreated illness can harm both mother and baby. The safe rule is simple: before starting, stopping, mixing, or changing any medicine, ask a doctor, nurse, or pharmacist who knows pregnancy and breastfeeding safety. Keep a list of everything you take. Careful medicine use protects two lives.

Chapter 181: Violence, Force, and Unsafe Home Situations

My dear,

Pregnancy does not protect every woman. Some women face hitting, pushing, forced sex, threats, fear, money control, or pressure to become pregnant or avoid family planning. This is abuse. It can harm the mother's body, mind, pregnancy, and baby. Belly injury, stress, poor sleep, bleeding, depression, and delayed care may follow. A woman should know this clearly: abuse is not her fault. She deserves safety, respect, and help. If a home is unsafe, tell a trusted health worker, doctor, nurse, friend, or relative. Ask for private help if speaking openly is dangerous. Emergency danger needs urgent action. Pregnancy care should include safety at home, not only blood pressure and scans.

Chapter 182: Newborn Danger Signs at Home

My dear,

I am your delivery nurse. You are like my daughter. I want to tell you the danger signs in a newborn baby at home. A newborn can become very sick very quickly. Seek help urgently if the baby is not feeding well, is too sleepy to wake for feeds, breathes fast, makes grunting sounds, looks blue, feels very hot or cold, has repeated vomiting, convulsions, fewer wet diapers, or worsening yellow color. Chapter 184: Pitocin Injection: When Labour Is Started or Strengthened

My dear,

Pitocin is a medicine that acts like the body's labour hormone and helps the womb tighten. Doctors may use it to start labour, strengthen weak pains, or reduce bleeding after birth, depending on the situation. It must be given carefully, not casually. While it is running, the mother's pains, the baby's heartbeat, and labour progress are watched closely. If contractions become too strong, too frequent, or the baby shows stress, the dose may need changing or stopping. Pitocin can be very helpful, but it is not a magic shortcut. Chapter 185: Vacuum Delivery: When Suction Helps Bring the Baby Out

My dear,

In some births, the baby is low in the birth passage, but extra help is needed to bring the baby out safely. A soft cup is placed on the baby's head, and gentle suction is used while the mother pushes during contractions. This is called vacuum delivery. It is not used in every labour. It is chosen only in selected situations, such as prolonged second stage, maternal exhaustion, or concern about the baby, when conditions are suitable. The mother should be told why it is advised. Chapter 186: Forceps Delivery: When Special Instruments Help Birth

My dear,

Forceps are metal instruments shaped to fit around the baby's head. In some difficult births, when the baby is low and the mother needs extra help, forceps may be used to guide the baby out during contractions and pushing. This method is not common in every labour and should be used only by trained doctors in the right situation. The mother should know why it is being considered and what other options exist. Forceps can help when quick delivery is needed or when vacuum is not suitable. Chapter 187: High Blood Pressure in Pregnancy

My dear,

Some women already have high pressure before pregnancy. Others develop it during pregnancy. Both need careful watching because high pressure can harm the mother, the placenta, and the baby's growth. Sometimes there are no symptoms at all, which is why regular checks matter so much. Some women get headache, blurred vision, swelling, pain under the ribs, or reduced baby movement. Chapter 188: Preeclampsia: Dangerous Pressure, Swelling, and Warning Signs

This is a dangerous pregnancy condition in which blood pressure becomes high and the body starts showing signs of strain, often including protein in the urine, swelling, headache, or changes in blood tests. Some women also get pain under the ribs, blurred vision, vomiting, or sudden puffiness of face and hands. Preeclampsia can affect the brain, kidneys, liver, placenta, and baby's growth. Chapter 189: Eclampsia: Fits in Pregnancy or After Birth

My dear,

Eclampsia means a woman with pregnancy-related high blood pressure develops fits or convulsions. This is a medical emergency. It can happen during pregnancy, during labour, or after birth. Before fits, some women get severe headache, blurred vision, flashing lights, confusion, vomiting, swelling, or pain under the ribs, but sometimes fits come suddenly. The mother and baby both face serious danger. Immediate hospital treatment is needed. The mother may need medicine to stop fits, blood pressure control, close monitoring, and urgent delivery if still pregnant. Family members should never put objects into her mouth during a fit. Protect her from injury, turn her safely to the side if possible, and get urgent help. Fast skilled care can save the mother's brain, organs, and baby.

Chapter 190: Gestational Diabetes: High Sugar During Pregnancy

My dear,

Some women feel normal and still have it, which is why testing is important. Management often includes diet changes, regular meals, walking, checking blood sugar, and sometimes medicine or insulin. This condition is not a punishment and not a reason for shame. It is a health problem that needs proper care. The mother should attend follow-up, follow food advice honestly, and not depend on myths. Careful treatment protects the baby's growth and supports a safer pregnancy, birth, and recovery.

Chapter 191: Constipation in Pregnancy and After Birth

My dear,

Many women get hard stool, difficulty passing motion, bloating, and pain because hormones slow the bowel, the growing womb adds pressure, activity reduces, and iron tablets may worsen the problem. After birth, pain, fear of stitches, dehydration, and less movement can make constipation even harder. Do not ignore it until the stool becomes very painful. Drink enough water, eat fruits, vegetables, fiber-rich foods, and walk gently if allowed. Do not strain too much. Passing urine and stool regularly helps comfort and healing. Some women may need stool softeners on medical advice. Severe pain, bleeding, vomiting, or many days without stool needs review. Timely care makes recovery easier and more comfortable.

Chapter 192: Hemorrhoids (Piles) in Pregnancy and After Delivery

My dear,

These are swollen veins around the back passage. Pregnancy pressure, constipation, straining, and pushing during birth can make them appear or worsen. They may cause pain, itching, swelling, or bleeding during stool passing. Many women feel shy to mention them, but quiet suffering only makes life harder. Good care includes preventing constipation, drinking enough water, eating fiber-rich food, gentle walking, avoiding long straining, and keeping the area clean. Warm sitting baths may help some women. If pain is severe or bleeding is frequent, medical review is needed because not all bleeding from the back passage is piles. A woman should not feel embarrassed. Chapter 193: Anal Fissure: Pain and Bleeding While Passing Stool

My dear,

A fissure is a small tear in the skin of the back passage. It usually happens because hard stool stretches and injures the area. The pain can be sharp, burning, and frightening during or after passing stool. Some women also see small bleeding on the tissue or in the pan. Pregnancy and the time after birth increase the risk because constipation is common then. Fear of pain may make the woman avoid stool, which worsens the problem. The key treatment is soft stool, not repeated straining. Drink water, eat fiber-rich food, walk gently, and use medicines only if advised. Severe pain, persistent bleeding, or long-lasting fissure needs medical review. Early treatment prevents a small tear from becoming a bigger problem.

Chapter 194: Thrombophlebitis: Painful Clot in a Surface Vein

My dear,

This means a vein becomes inflamed, and often a small clot forms inside it. It usually affects a surface vein, often in the leg. The area may look red, feel warm, tender, hard, or swollen like a painful cord under the skin. It may happen more easily in pregnancy or after birth because blood clots form more easily then. Rest, movement advice, stockings, pain relief, and medical review may be needed. Sometimes a scan is done to check that the clot is not deeper. Do not massage a painful swollen leg. Seek urgent help if swelling spreads, pain becomes severe, or breathing trouble starts. A leg clot may look small, but it should never be ignored. Early review protects the mother from more dangerous blood-clot problems.

Chapter 195: Pulmonary Embolism: A Clot Reaching the Lungs

My dear,

This happens when a blood clot, often from the leg, travels to the lungs. It is a life-threatening emergency in pregnancy and after birth. Warning signs include sudden shortness of breath, sharp chest pain, coughing, coughing blood, feeling faint, fast heartbeat, or sudden collapse. Some women first notice a painful swollen leg before breathing symptoms begin. Never wait at home with these signs.

Fast treatment can save life. Sudden chest pain or breathlessness after leg pain, after surgery, or after birth must always be treated as an emergency.

When to seek help: Go urgently. Pregnancy and the weeks after birth increase the risk of dangerous clots, so early action matters. Doctors may do blood tests, scans, oxygen checks, and start blood-thinning treatment quickly.

Chapter 196: Antibiotics in Pregnancy and Breastfeeding

My dear,

Antibiotics are medicines used to treat bacterial infection. They can be very important when there is urine infection, wound infection, chest infection, breast infection, fever after birth, or certain labour situations. But not every fever needs an antibiotic, and not every antibiotic is right for every mother. Some are safer than others in pregnancy and while feeding. That is why these medicines should be chosen by a doctor. The full course should be taken exactly as advised. Stopping early may make the infection return. Never take leftover tablets from someone else. Also do not refuse an antibiotic out of fear. Untreated infection can be more dangerous than the medicine. Right antibiotic, right reason, right dose, and right duration protect both mother and baby.

Chapter 197: Antidepressant Medicines in Pregnancy and After Birth

My dear,

These medicines are used when depression or anxiety is harming the mother's sleep, appetite, hope, daily life, bonding, or safety. Some women need talking therapy alone. Some need medicine too. The decision should be personal and made with a doctor who understands pregnancy and breastfeeding. Stopping medicine suddenly can cause harm. Untreated depression itself can affect the mother, the baby, feeding, and family life. So the question is not only, Is medicine risky? The question is, What is safest overall for this mother? Chapter 198: Painkillers, Cold Medicines, and Home Remedies

My dear,

Chapter 199: Bleeding in Early Pregnancy: What It Can Mean

My dear,

A little spotting can happen in some women and does not always mean miscarriage. But bleeding should never be dismissed without thought. The amount, colour, pain, and timing all matter. Light spotting may settle. Heavy bleeding, strong cramps, one-sided pain, dizziness, fainting, or shoulder pain need urgent medical review. These signs may mean miscarriage, pregnancy outside the womb, or another problem. The doctor may do an ultrasound, blood tests, or repeat checks. Do not insert anything into the birth passage, do not take random medicines, and do not blame yourself. Chapter 200: Miscarriage: Why It Happens and What Care May Be Needed

My dear,

Miscarriage means the pregnancy stops growing and ends before the baby can live outside the womb. It is sadly common, especially in the first months, and often happens because the pregnancy was not developing normally. Bleeding and cramping are common signs. Tissue or clots may also pass. Some women feel only light symptoms at first, so ultrasound and blood tests may be needed. Treatment depends on what is happening. Sometimes the body passes the pregnancy naturally. Sometimes medicine is used. Sometimes a procedure is needed. The right option depends on bleeding, pain, infection risk, and the woman's wishes. Miscarriage is not caused by normal movement, ordinary stress, or one small mistake. Emotional healing also matters after the body's loss and pain.

Chapter 201: Repeated Miscarriage: Low Thyroid and Antiphospholipid Syndrome

My dear,

When a woman has two or more miscarriages, doctors usually advise a checkup. The aim is not blame. The aim is to look for treatable causes. Two important causes are low thyroid and antiphospholipid syndrome. Low thyroid means the thyroid gland is not making enough hormone, and that can affect pregnancy if not treated properly. Antiphospholipid syndrome is a blood-clotting and immune condition that can increase miscarriage risk. Some women may also need checks for diabetes, womb shape problems, or chromosome issues in the parents. Not every repeated miscarriage has a clear reason, but evaluation is still worthwhile. Honest testing, proper treatment where possible, and compassionate follow-up can help many women try again more safely.

Chapter 202: Pregnancy Outside the Womb: A Dangerous Emergency

My dear,

This is called ectopic pregnancy. It happens when the pregnancy grows in the tube or another place instead of inside the womb. The tube cannot safely hold a growing pregnancy, so this can become a life-threatening emergency. Warning signs include one-sided lower tummy pain, bleeding, shoulder pain, dizziness, fainting, or sudden worsening pain. A home pregnancy test may still be positive, so a positive test alone does not prove the pregnancy is in the right place. The doctor may need ultrasound and blood tests to find the cause. Treatment may be medicine or surgery, depending on the stage and the mother's condition. Quick action can save the mother's life and future fertility in some cases.

Chapter 203: Placenta Previa: When the Placenta Lies Low

My dear,

This means the baby's feeding organ lies low in the womb and partly or fully covers the mouth of the womb. Because of this, painless bleeding can happen in later pregnancy. Sometimes the bleeding is light at first, then becomes heavier later. A woman with bleeding in pregnancy should always be checked quickly. Placenta previa is usually found by ultrasound. If it is present, vaginal examination may be avoided unless the team is ready and the diagnosis is clear, because bleeding risk matters. The mother may need rest advice, hospital care, repeat scans, and careful birth planning. Heavy bleeding is an emergency. In many cases, cesarean birth is the safer route. Calm monitoring and good planning protect mother and baby both.

Chapter 204: Heavy Bleeding After Birth (PPH): Fast Action Saves Life

My dear,

This is called postpartum hemorrhage, or PPH, meaning dangerous blood loss after delivery. It can happen soon after the baby is born or later. The mother may bleed heavily, pass large clots, feel dizzy, faint, weak, restless, or breathless. The womb may feel soft instead of firm. Causes include poor womb tightening, tears, placenta pieces left inside, or clotting problems. PPH is an emergency. The team acts quickly with womb massage, medicines, fluids, blood if needed, and finding the cause. A woman should never think heavy bleeding is normal because birth just happened. Fast action saves life, protects organs, and prevents shock. After birth, watching bleeding closely is one of the most important parts of care.

Chapter 205: Retained Placenta and Ongoing Bleeding After Delivery

My dear,

This means the baby's feeding organ, or part of it, does not come out completely after birth. When this happens, the mother may bleed more, the womb may not tighten well, and later she may get pain, fever, or foul discharge. Sometimes the placenta is stuck, trapped, or only pieces remain inside. This is not a problem to ignore. The mother may need urgent treatment, medicine, or a procedure to remove what is left. Ongoing bleeding after delivery is always a warning sign, not something to watch casually at home. Good examination of the placenta after birth helps catch this early. Early treatment prevents infection, severe blood loss, and later illness.

Chapter 206: Baby Blues After Delivery: Normal Emotional Ups and Downs

My dear,

In the first days after birth, many mothers cry easily, feel emotional, become sensitive, or feel suddenly overwhelmed. This is common and is called baby blues. It usually starts in the first few days and improves within about two weeks. The mother may still love her baby and care for the baby, but she feels more tearful than usual. Hormone changes, pain, exhaustion, poor sleep, and the huge life change all play a part. Baby blues are not weakness and not bad motherhood. The mother needs rest, nourishment, reassurance, and help with the baby. Family should be gentle, not critical. If sadness becomes severe or lasts longer, she needs more help.

Chapter 207: Postpartum Depression: When Sadness Lasts and Needs Help

My dear,

This is more serious than baby blues. The mother may feel deep sadness, hopelessness, guilt, fear, emptiness, poor sleep even when the baby sleeps, loss of interest, poor bonding, or thoughts that she is a bad mother. These feelings may last longer and disturb daily life. Postpartum depression is a medical condition, not laziness or weakness. It can happen to loving mothers. The mother needs support, honest listening, and professional help. Treatment may include counseling, support, and sometimes medicine. Early help protects both mother and baby, because untreated depression affects feeding, rest, bonding, and safety. Chapter 208: Postpartum Psychosis: A Rare but Urgent Mental Emergency

My dear,

This is rare, but it is a true emergency. The mother may become very confused, unable to sleep at all, fearful, suspicious, extremely overexcited, or disconnected from reality. She may hear voices, see things, speak strangely, or have frightening thoughts about herself or the baby. This is not normal tiredness or simple sadness. Family members must act fast and not feel ashamed to seek emergency care. Quick treatment can save life and protect both mother and child. Chapter 209: Newborn Jaundice in the First 24 Hours: Why It Is Urgent

My dear,

Jaundice means yellowing of the baby's skin or eyes because bilirubin is rising in the blood. Some jaundice is common later, but jaundice appearing in the first day is more worrying and needs urgent medical review. It can point to blood group problems, infection, internal bleeding, or other serious causes. The baby may also be sleepy or feed poorly. Parents should never wait at home with yellow color that starts very early. The baby may need blood tests, close observation, and treatment such as phototherapy. Early jaundice is not a small matter. Chapter 210: Newborn Jaundice from Day 1 to Day 3

My dear,

Many babies become a little yellow in these days because their bodies are adjusting and clearing bilirubin more slowly. This can be common, but it still needs watching. The baby should feed well, pass urine and stool, wake for feeds, and not become too sleepy. Good feeding helps bilirubin leave the body. If the yellow color deepens quickly, reaches the legs early, or the baby feeds poorly, seems floppy, or is hard to wake, medical review is needed. Some babies need blood tests and treatment. Do not rely only on room light or family opinion. Early checking is safer. Jaundice in these days may be normal or may need help. Careful watching protects the baby from silent harm.

Chapter 211: Newborn Jaundice After 7 Days: When to Keep Watching

My dear,

Sometimes yellow color fades, but sometimes it remains. In a breastfed baby, mild jaundice may continue longer and still be harmless, but it should never be guessed at home without review. The baby's feeding, weight gain, stools, urine color, activity, and overall health all matter. If the baby is sleepy, not gaining weight, has pale stools, dark urine, fever, poor feeding, or deeper yellow color, the doctor should check the baby soon. Jaundice after one week may still be simple, but sometimes it points to infection, blood problems, liver trouble, or other causes. Continued yellow color needs thoughtful assessment, not fear and not neglect.

Chapter 212: Jaundice That Lasts Up to 30 Days: When It Needs Further Checking

My dear,

Jaundice lasting this long should not be ignored, even if the baby seems otherwise well. These include liver or bile flow problems, infection, blood breakdown, thyroid problems, or other medical conditions. The baby may need blood tests and careful follow-up. Pale or chalk-colored stools and dark urine are especially important warning signs. A growing baby with persistent jaundice still deserves assessment. Parents should keep feeding, keep appointments, and watch the baby's alertness, stools, urine, and weight. Timely review helps detect rare but serious illness before delay causes more harm.

Chapter 213: Phototherapy: Blue-Light Treatment for Jaundice Made Simple

My dear,

Phototherapy is the blue-light treatment used for some babies with jaundice. The light helps change bilirubin into a form the baby's body can remove more easily. It is a common and important treatment. The baby is placed under special lights with the eyes protected, and the team keeps checking temperature, feeding, hydration, and bilirubin levels. Parents may feel frightened seeing the baby under lights, but this treatment can prevent serious harm when bilirubin is too high. Feeding should continue because good hydration helps. Some babies need short treatment, some longer. Phototherapy is not punishment and does not mean the baby is very weak. It is used to protect the brain and body.

Chapter 214: Thalassemia Trait, Thalassemia Major, and Pregnancy Planning

My dear,

Thalassemia is an inherited blood condition. A person with thalassemia trait often looks healthy but carries the gene. If both parents carry thalassemia trait, the baby can be born with thalassemia major, which is a severe illness needing repeated treatment and blood transfusions. That is why simple blood testing before or during pregnancy matters. Screening helps couples understand risk early. If both are carriers, they need counseling about what this means for the baby and the family. This is not about blame. It is about informed planning. A woman with thalassemia herself also needs careful pregnancy care because anemia and other problems may be greater. Knowing carrier status early gives families time for calm decisions.

Chapter 215: Sickle Cell Trait, Sickle Cell Disease, and the Baby's Blood Tests

My dear,

Sickle cell is an inherited blood disorder. A person with the trait usually carries the gene but may not have the full disease. A person with sickle cell disease can become very unwell and needs specialist care. If both parents carry the gene, the baby may be affected. That is why blood testing before or during pregnancy is important. Newborn blood spot screening can also help identify affected babies early, so treatment and infection protection can begin. Early diagnosis saves lives. Parents should understand that carrier status is not a weakness and not a moral fault. Honest testing and counseling help families prepare wisely. Early detection in the baby means better protection.

Chapter 216: Hole in the Heart: VSD and ASD in Simple Words

My dear,

VSD means a hole between the two lower pumping chambers of the heart. ASD means a hole between the two upper chambers. Some small holes cause few problems and may close on their own. Some larger holes can cause poor feeding, fast breathing, poor weight gain, repeated chest infection, or tiredness. Not every hole in the heart turns the baby blue. Some are found only because the doctor hears a murmur and orders a scan of the heart. Parents should not panic immediately, but they should also not ignore follow-up. A heart specialist may watch the baby over time and decide if medicine or treatment is needed. Early diagnosis helps the child grow better.

Chapter 217: Blue Baby Heart Problems: When Low Oxygen Turns the Baby Blue

My dear,

This phrase is used when a baby looks bluish because the blood is not getting enough oxygen. Some serious heart defects can cause this, especially when blood flow through the heart and lungs is abnormal. A baby may look blue around the lips and tongue, breathe fast, feed poorly, or become tired very quickly. Blue color in a newborn is never something to ignore. Some heart problems are found during pregnancy scans, some are found after birth by examination or low oxygen readings. The baby may need urgent assessment, oxygen monitoring, heart scan, and specialist care. Fast recognition matters because some babies become suddenly worse. Blue baby, poor feeding, or fast breathing needs urgent medical help without delay.

Chapter 218: Baby Checks at Birth: Apgar, Oxygen Test, Blood Spot, Hearing, and Examination

My dear,

Soon after birth, the baby is examined to see breathing, color, heart rate, muscle tone, and response. This quick early check is often called the Apgar score. The baby is also examined from head to toe for any visible problem. In many places, hearing screening, blood spot screening, and pulse oximetry are also done later to look for hidden conditions. Pulse oximetry is a simple oxygen check that can help detect some serious heart problems early. Blood spot screening can look for certain inherited or metabolic conditions. These tests do not mean something is wrong. They are safety checks. Early detection allows early treatment. Simple screening can protect the baby from hidden illness.

Chapter 219: Injections and Vaccines at Birth: Vitamin K, Hepatitis B, and Other Early Protection

My dear,

One important injection is vitamin K. This helps protect the baby from dangerous bleeding because newborn babies have low vitamin K stores. Another important protection is the hepatitis B vaccine, which is given at birth in many programs to reduce early infection risk. Depending on the country and situation, other routine checks and protections may also be planned. Parents should understand that these early treatments are given to prevent serious problems before they happen. They are not unnecessary pain. Vitamin K helps prevent bleeding in the brain or body. Birth vaccines help build protection early. The baby should also be kept warm, fed, and monitored. Asking questions is good, but delaying proven protection can increase avoidable risk.

Chapter 220: SIDS: Sudden Sleep Death in Babies

My dear,

SIDS means sudden infant death syndrome. It refers to the sudden and unexpected death of a baby, usually during sleep, when no clear cause is found even after careful review. This is rare, but families should know the main ways to reduce risk. Put the baby to sleep on the back, not on the tummy or side. Use a firm flat sleep surface. Keep pillows, loose blankets, soft toys, and heavy bedding away from the baby. Do not let the baby sleep in a smoky room. Avoid overheating. Bed-sharing can increase risk in some situations, especially if adults smoke, drink alcohol, use drugs, or are extremely tired. Safe sleep habits matter every day. A sleeping baby should look peaceful, but the sleep space must also be planned carefully.

Chapter 221: Smoking, Secondhand Smoke, and Why They Increase Baby Risk

My dear,

Smoking during pregnancy harms the mother, the placenta, and the growing baby. It increases the risk of poor baby growth, early birth, placenta problems, stillbirth, and breathing trouble. Smoke around the newborn after birth is also dangerous. It irritates the baby's lungs and increases the risk of chest illness and sudden infant death. A mother should not smoke, but the home also needs protection from other people's smoke. Fathers and relatives matter here. A baby cannot choose the air it breathes. Smoking outside is better than inside, but the safest home is a smoke-free home. Clothes and hands should also be clean before holding the baby after smoking. Protecting the baby from smoke is a loving act.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 222: Safe Sleep for the Newborn: Back to Sleep, Clear Cot, No Smoke

My dear,

A baby should be placed on the back for every sleep, day and night. The sleep surface should be firm, flat, and free from pillows, soft toys, heavy blankets, and loose cloth. The baby should not sleep in a smoky room. Overheating should be avoided. Room-sharing with the parents can help safety, but the baby should usually have a separate safe sleep space. If adults smoke, drink alcohol, use sedating medicines, or are very tired, bed-sharing becomes more risky. A newborn may look tiny and peaceful, but sleep safety must be planned carefully every time. Back to sleep, clear cot, no smoke, and no soft bedding are simple rules that protect life.

Chapter 223: Anemia in Pregnancy: Blood Weakness That Needs Attention

My dear,

Anemia means the blood has less hemoglobin than needed to carry oxygen well. Iron deficiency is a common cause. Symptoms may include tiredness, weakness, dizziness, paleness, headache, breathlessness, poor concentration, or fast heartbeat. Severe anemia increases danger if bleeding happens at delivery and may affect the baby's growth. Doctors check hemoglobin level and decide if anemia is mild, moderate, or severe. Treatment may be iron tablets, syrup, or iron injections, depending on level, symptoms, and how well the stomach tolerates treatment. Iron is often absorbed better away from milk, calcium, tea, coffee, and heavy food. Black stool is common and usually harmless. If iron causes acidity, ask how to take it better. Chapter 224: Folic Acid, Calcium, Iron, and Other Helpful Supplements

Folic acid is a vitamin that helps protect the baby's brain and spine, so it is best started before pregnancy and continued in the early months. Iron helps build blood and prevent anemia. Calcium supports bones, muscles, teeth, and healthy body function. Some women also need vitamin D so the body can use calcium properly. These supplements are not decorations. They protect the mother and the growing baby. Iron and calcium are often taken at different times because calcium can reduce iron absorption. Do not stop supplements because of myths or mild discomfort. Ask how to take them better. Good supplements, along with food and follow-up, build a safer pregnancy and a stronger mother.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 225: Medicines to Strictly Avoid or Never Self-Start in Pregnancy

My dear,

Do not take acne medicine containing retinoic acid or isotretinoin. This medicine can seriously harm the baby, and pregnancy must be avoided for a period before trying to conceive after isotretinoin treatment. Some hormone medicines and steroids also need medical supervision and should never be started casually. NSAID painkillers, such as ibuprofen-like drugs, are usually avoided in the third trimester because they can harm the baby and affect blood flow. Metronidazole should not be self-started in the first trimester; use it only if a doctor decides it is needed. Antibiotics are not all the same. The safest rule is simple: no self-medication in pregnancy. Always ask before taking anything.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 226: Urine Infection in Pregnancy

My dear,

Some women feel burning, frequent urination, lower tummy discomfort, fever, or back pain. But some urine infections cause no clear symptoms at all and are found only by testing. Even silent infection matters in pregnancy because it can spread, make the mother unwell, and increase risk of problems if untreated. That is why urine testing is useful. Drink enough water and do not hold urine for too long. Wiping cleanly and emptying the bladder regularly can help reduce risk. But home care alone is not enough when infection is present. The mother may need antibiotics chosen carefully for pregnancy. Fever, back pain, vomiting, or feeling very ill needs urgent review. Timely treatment protects the kidneys, the pregnancy, and the baby.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 227: Reduced Baby Movements: What to Do the Same Day

My dear,

I am your delivery nurse. You are like my daughter. I want to tell you what to do if baby movements become less. First, do not panic, but do not ignore it. Go somewhere quiet, have something to eat or drink, lie on your side, and pay attention to the baby's movements. Many babies have sleep times, but a baby that is truly moving less than usual needs same-day review. Do not wait for the next morning if the pattern feels changed. Reduced movement can be a warning sign that the baby needs checking. The doctor or nurse may listen to the heartbeat, use CTG, or do other tests. Trust your own noticing. Mothers often sense change early. Even if the baby turns out fine, it was still right to seek help. It is always safer to be checked than to stay worried and delay care.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Chapter 228: Breast Problems After Birth: Engorgement, Blocked Duct, and Mastitis

My dear,

Many mothers get engorgement, meaning the breasts become overly full, hard, heavy, and painful when milk builds up. Some get blocked ducts, which cause a tender lump. Some develop mastitis, with fever, redness, body ache, and stronger breast pain. These problems do not mean the mother has failed. They mean feeding needs support. Good latch, frequent feeding, emptying the breast well, rest, and fluids help many mothers. A blocked area should not be ignored. Fever and redness need quick review because infection may need treatment. Stopping all feeding suddenly can make things worse. Ask for help early. Timely guidance protects milk flow, reduces pain, and helps the mother continue feeding with greater comfort and confidence.

A Final Word

You have now travelled through the full journey, from the first quiet suspicion of good news, through every month of pregnancy, through labour and birth, through recovery and newborn care, and through the decisions that protect your family's future. That is a journey of courage, love, patience, and learning. You have done something important simply by choosing to understand.

Pregnancy is not only a physical event. It is the beginning of a lifelong relationship between a mother and her child, between a family and its future. The care you gave yourself during these months, the questions you asked, the help you sought early, the rest you allowed yourself, all of that was an act of love toward the small life that depended on you.

When something feels uncertain, return to this book. When something feels urgent, put this book down and go to a doctor. Books are companions for learning. Doctors are companions for crisis. Know the difference and use both wisely.

You are not alone. You were never alone. Your health matters. Your baby's health matters. And every small act of self-care you gave yourself was the first gift you gave your child.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

Epilogue

You Were Never Alone

The first day you held a positive test in your hands, your whole life changed in one moment. One small line. One word. Yes. And with that one word, everything you thought you knew about yourself was quietly rearranged.

You were afraid. That is the truth no one says aloud. Even the mothers who smiled the widest were afraid. Afraid of the unknown body. Afraid of the weight of love that had not yet arrived but was already enormous. Afraid of doing it wrong. Afraid of the pain. Afraid of becoming someone new when the old you still felt unfinished.

This book walked beside you through all of it. Through the nausea that came without warning at 3pm and at midnight. Through the appointments where you sat quietly hoping the heartbeat would be there, then felt the tears come when it was. Through the middle months when the baby moved and you lay still in the dark pressing your hand to your belly and felt, for the first time, that you were two.

You may have read these chapters at the kitchen table in the early morning when the house was still sleeping. You may have read them in the waiting room of a clinic, finding the right words for what you were feeling. You may have read them through tears, or through sleepiness, or quietly, one paragraph at a time, while someone you loved sat nearby without knowing how much you needed the company.

Here is what this book wanted you to know from the very first page.

You are not a patient moving through a system. You are a woman carrying a universe. You are not a body to be monitored. You are a mind to be respected, a heart to be heard, a story to be honored.

Your body was not wrong when it was afraid. It was honest. Your heart was not weak when it broke with love before the baby even arrived. It was already mothering. Your voice was not small when you asked for help. It was the bravest thing you did.

The world will not always stop to see how hard this was. The world moves fast and expects mothers to move with it. But this book sees you. Every chapter was written for the woman who is doing her absolute best with everything she has, which has always been enough, and always will be.

Your baby will not remember the ward where they were born, the medicine that was given, the hours that were hard. They will remember arms. Warmth. A voice that came from somewhere familiar before they even had words for familiar. That voice is yours. It always has been.

You grew a person. You brought a life through your body and into the world. And now you will spend the rest of your life learning how to love in a way you never knew was possible.

There is nothing left to do now except begin.

Go gently. Ask for help early. Trust your body when it speaks. Trust your love when it feels too large to hold. It is large enough. You are large enough.

You always were.
